20241017195334.an:
During approach to land with the autopilot engaged, in visual meteorological conditions, the airplane struck an object while at a height of about 1,540 ft above the ground, and at a speed of about 170 knots, as the airplane began a left turn toward the final approach course. Just prior to the strike, the pilot briefly saw a white object through the right (copilot side) windscreen, which he initially surmised was a bird. He described the impact as an “extremely loud” booming noise and was like hitting a “Mack truck”. He checked the windscreen for damage and confirmed that the airframe parachute system had not deployed. 

The airplane’s Emergency Autoland (EA) system had activated, likely due to the collision, and he overheard repeating automated emergency radio transmissions in his headset announcing the airplane’s callsign and declaring an emergency (a function of the EA). These transmissions interfered with his communications with the air traffic control tower, and his initial attempts to deactivate the EA system by pressing the autopilot disconnect button (AP DISC) several times, were unsuccessful. 

He noticed damage to copilot side sun visor, the copilot side oxygen mask had fallen from its stowed position, a fire extinguishing switch was damaged, the cabin pressure dump switch had activated, and the transponder had changed to the emergency code of 7700 (another feature of the EA system). On-board recorded data indicated that the EA system was ultimately deactivated, though the pilot was unsure if or when it had. He reported that he had no difficulty controlling the airplane, which responded to his flight control inputs as well as flap and landing gear selections, when and as expected. He was able to land the airplane without further incident. 

Postlanding photographs showed white, red, and blue paint transfer marks leading from the lower left edge to the upper center of the right windscreen, which was inconsistent with a bird strike. The object struck was not identified, as explained later below.
The airplane’s on-board recorded data indicated that the EA system had activated twice, in succession. The data indicated neither of the autopilot modes that are a prerequisite for an automatic activation of EA were engaged either time, suggesting that the activations were initiated by the manual button in the overhead panel. 

The first activation occurred nearly simultaneously (within 1 second or less) when the cabin pressure dump system activated, and likely at the same time as the equipment disturbances in and near the overhead panel. This, along with 1) post accident testing of an exemplar EA button revealed that it would activate when subjected to shock and 2) the pilot’s testimony that he never pressed the EA button, suggests that the first EA activation was most likely due to a shock load to the button during the object strike. 

However, the on-board recording system did not detect a signal from the button at that time. This was likely due to the recorder’s 1 second sample rate for the EA button status. The EA button (as well as the AP DISC button) is a spring-loaded momentary contact type, which does not remain pressed or latched when pushed. A brief actuation of either of these buttons, shorter than 1 second, may not be detected by the recording system. 

About 10 seconds after the first EA activation, the recording system detected a signal from the AP DISC button for a single recoding sample. However, the EA did not deactivate. Post incident research and testing by the airframe manufacturer using exemplar avionics revealed two repeatable software defects related to the AP DISC button function. 

First, the AP DISC button had no effect if pressed during a certain unquantified period of time between about 8-10 seconds after the start of an EA activation. This may explain why the EA system did not deactivate in response to the (single) recorded AP DISC button press. The AP DISC button status was also recorded at a 1 second sample rate. Had the pilot pressed the AP DISC button more than once during the ‘defect’ period, it would likely not have deactivated EA. Further, multiple brief presses of the AP DISC button could have occurred and not been recorded due to the 1 second sample rate. 

Second, the aural autopilot disconnect warning tone, which is normally sounded through the airplane’s audio system whenever the autopilot is disconnected, would not sound if the AP DISC button was pressed at any time while EA was active. 

The on-board recorded data indicated that first EA activation was terminated about 20 seconds after it began. This may have been in response to a press of the AP DISC button by the pilot, but if so, the press must have been too brief and between recording samples, as none were recorded. The second EA activation began about 3 seconds after the first one was terminated. At that time, the recoded data captured a signal from the EA button, indicating it had activated. Examination of the EA button assembly did not reveal any obvious damage, though the button was found to be “slightly loose” compared to an exemplar unit. As noted above, an exemplar button was found to be susceptible to activation when shocked, however no apparent source of shock was identified at the time of the 2nd activation. 

The pilot was adamant in his interview that he did not press the button at any time. The investigation was unable to determine what led to the 2nd button activation. This EA activation was terminated about 20 seconds after it began, and the recording system did not detect a press of the AP DISC button. As noted above, it is possible for brief press of the AP DISC button to not be recorded, however this could not be confirmed. 

The investigation was unable to identify the object that collided with the incident airplane. The potential for collision with an unmanned aircraft system (e.g. drone, model aircraft) or an experimental balloon were considered. 

The strike occurred about 30 seconds after the airplane passed by a hobbyist remote control model aircraft field, which was an FAA approved location for unmanned aircraft system (UAS) operations. At the time of the strike, the airplane was 1.8 nm northwest of the model aircraft field, at an altitude of 1,540 ft above the ground. This was well outside the field’s lateral dimensions, and about 1,140 ft above its 400 ft altitude restriction. Given the lateral distance from the model aircraft field, it is unlikely that a remote pilot located at the model aircraft field was operating a UAS flying at the location of the strike, with direct visual observation of the UAS (by either a remote pilot or a visual observer), as required by the FAA and the model aircraft club operating rules. 

The safety officer for the model aircraft field reported that a polling of club members revealed no known conflicts with the incident airplane. Whether or not a UAS was being operated from the model aircraft field or from any other location, either without direct visual observation, or because of a lost radio communication, could not be determined from the available evidence. 

While the FAA requires that some UAS be operated with a remote identification (RID) system, a representative from the FAA reported that:
 
there are no archived flights of drones or RID broadcasts
remote pilots do not file flight plans
Drones are not equipped with radar transponders
neither drones nor RID message elements appear on air traffic control radar displays 

The Civil Air Patrol, which had previously launched some experimental balloons from various locations in and around Austin, reported that they had not conducted any launches on the day of the incident.
20241017195334.fa:
On September 14, 2024, at 1248 central daylight time, a Cirrus SF50, N442CV, experienced an unintended activation of its Emergency Autoland (EA) system at or near the time the airplane was struck by an unknown object during approach into Austin Bergstrom International Airport (AUS), Austin, Texas. The airplane sustained minor damage due to the impact, and the pilot was not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight from Cincinnati Municipal Airport/Lunken Field (LUK), Cincinnati, Ohio to AUS.

Object Strike
According to the pilot, during a left turn toward the final approach course, with the autopilot engaged, he briefly saw a white object through the right windscreen and then heard an “extremely loud” booming noise. He further described it as sounding like he “hit a Mack truck”. He later noticed that several items in or near the overhead panels were disturbed. The right-side sun visor had broken, and the copilot oxygen mask fell from its stowage area. 

The cabin pressure dump switch had activated, and one of the “PUSH to DISCHARGE” fire bottle activation buttons had separated from the overhead panel and fell to the floor. The manual EA activation button was located overhead in a panel just aft of the disturbed items. The EA system was designed to autonomously land the airplane, in the event of pilot incapacitation. It can be manually activated via this button, or in some situations can be automatically activated as described later below. Once activated, it manages airplane control, navigation, emergency radio and transponder communications to land at the nearest appropriate airport. 

Figure 1. Overhead Panel. (Source: Cirrus Aircraft)

The pilot initially thought that the airframe parachute had deployed. After he noticed that the copilot side sun visor was damaged, he checked the windscreen for damage (it was scratched but intact), and the parachute status, to determine if it had deployed (it had not). He then heard an automated voice in his headset that was repeating the airplane’s callsign (N442CV) and declaring an emergency, which was his first indication that EA had activated (this automated radio transmission is part of the programmed sequence of events that occur when the after EA is activated). 

As the automated radio transmissions occurred, they prevented him from communicating with the AUS air traffic control tower. He also noticed that the transponder had been set to squawk 7700 (another item in the EA activation sequence) and the control tower confirmed receiving 7700. He recalled that he had repeatedly pressed the autopilot (AP) disconnect button, however the automated radio transmissions repeated 3-4 times before they eventually stopped. 

He was then able to inform the tower that he was able to make a normal landing and receive landing clearance. The remainder of the flight was uneventful. After landing, the pilot wiped the airplane down and noted there was an “oily residue” on the windscreen. He did not retain any samples of the residue.  

The pilot surmised that the airplane had struck a bird. However, a photograph provided by the airplane manufacturer showed scrape marks and blue, red, and white color transfer marks that extended diagonally from the bottom of the right windscreen near the center post toward the top and outboard side the windscreen, see figure 2. 

Figure 2. Scrape and color transfer on windscreen. (Source: Cirrus Aircraft)

A review of Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) automatic dependent surveillance broadcast (ADS-B) airplane tracking data, revealed that the airplane had flown past the Austin Radio Control Association (ACRA) model aircraft field, located about 8 nautical miles northeast of AUS. As the airplane flew to the west on a track of about 268°, it was abeam the model aircraft field at 1247:08 which was about 0.65 nautical miles to the south. At that time the airplane’s altitude was about 2,300 ft above the ground, according to on-board recorded flight data from the airplane’s radio altimeter. 

Figure 3. Airplane track – (direction of flight was west followed by left turn to the south).
According to the ADS-B and on-board recorded flight data, the EA activation and cabin pressure dump system activation occurred about 30 seconds after the airplane passed by the model aircraft field, and at that time was about 1.8 nautical miles to the northwest. The EA function activated as the airplane was at a radio altitude of 1,540 ft above the ground at speed of 167 knots. Figure 4 shows the location of the activation relative to the model aircraft field location and size. 

Figure 4. Strike location. (Image source: FAA, annotation NTSB)

The safety officer from ACRA reported that they had polled their membership (about 120 total members, 20-30 of which fly on a regular basis), and none reported knowledge of, observing, or involvement with N442CV. They also advised that all ACRA operations of model aircraft, also known as unmanned aerial systems (UAS) were, by the Academy of Model Aeronautics rules and federal aviation regulations, below 400 ft above ground level. Most of the members aircraft weigh under 15 lbs. and none exceed 35 lbs. 

In the event of a loss of radio communication, most of the aircraft flown at the field are configured to fly in a 360° circle and hold altitude, until a connection is re-established. First person view operations, in which the remote pilot uses goggles or a display to view video from an on-board camera (and not directly viewing the UAS from their position), are permitted at the field but require a second observer pilot to maintain direct view of the UAS at all times. 

The FAA requires that certain unmanned aircraft systems (UAS), including some hobby drones and model aircraft, be equipped with a remote ID (RID) device that broadcasts identification and aircraft position. RID is not required by the FAA for UAS operations within approved FAA-Recognized Identification Areas (of which ACRA was one) but does require that RID equipped UAS’s to have the RID operating while flying in such areas. A representative from the FAA reported that there was no archived data of any RID broadcasts available. 

Representatives from the Civil Air Patrol, which had previously launched some experimental balloons from various locations in Austin, reported that they had not conducted any launches on the day of the incident. 

Flight data were recovered from the N442CV’s central maintenance computer (CMC) and recoverable data module (RDM). The data showed that the EA system activated and deactivated twice in succession, however details about the initiation and termination of EA were not consistently captured in the recorded data. 

Emergency Autoland (EA) Activation and Deactivation

According to the airplane’s pilot information manual, EA (also referred to as “Safe Return Autoland”) can be activated by: 
1) Manually pressing the overhead EA pushbutton.
2) Automatically, if the autopilot’s “Automatic Level Mode” has been engaged for one minute.
3) Automatically, if the autopilot’s Emergency Descent Mode is engaged, and the airplane descends through 15,000 ft pressure altitude.

EA can be deactivated by:

1) Pressing either the left (pilot) or right (copilot) AP disconnect button located on the control stick for one second.

2) Pressing the AP button on the autopilot control unit in the instrument panel. 

According to the on-board recoded data, at 1247:38, while at an altitude of about 1,540 ft above ground level and at a speed of 167 knots, the automatic flight control system (AFCS) mode changed from “selected altitude” mode to “level” mode, and within one second, the recorded CMC parameter EMER AUTOLAND ACTIVATING parameter changed from FALSE to TRUE, indicating that EA waiting/warning period mode began, and a warning message was displayed on instrument panel advising of the activation.

In addition to this messaging, by design, the waiting/warning period lasts for 10 seconds, during which the autopilot will enter the “level” mode (as noted above), an automated audio cue announcing “Emergency Autoland Activating” will sound on the airplane’s audio system (through the headsets and cockpit speaker), and a visual annunciator next to the manual activation button will illuminate. The EA system will then wait until the end of the waiting/warning period, before activating other EA functions, including the automated radio calls and transponder tuning. 

However, at the time of EA initiation, there were no other indications in the CMC or RDM data that either of the two automatic means of initiation had occurred. Further, the RDM parameter that captured the status of the manual activation button did not indicate that the button had been pressed. The manual activation button is a spring-loaded momentary contact style, which after pressed, returns to its normal resting position. Additionally, the RDM parameter that records the button’s status (pressed or not pressed) is sampled at 1 Hz. As a result, if the button were pressed (or, activated by some other means, such as due to the collision) briefly, and between the 1 second samples, it may not have been captured in the recorded data. 

The data indicated that the waiting/warning period lasted for about 10 seconds, as designed. The CMC parameter that monitored the status of the autopilot disconnect (AP DISC) buttons, which were also momentary contact style and recorded at a rate of 1 Hz, indicated that AP DISC button was pressed during a single recorded sample at 1247:48, just prior to the end of the EA waiting/warning period. 

However, the EA system did not deactivate. After the waiting/warning period, the EA continued to the next phase of full activation and continued for another 10 seconds, before it was deactivated. The AP DISC parameter did not capture a button press at the time EA deactivated. 

About 3 seconds later, the EA waiting/warning period activated again, and this time the recorded data showed that the overhead manual activation button was pressed. The warning period was active for 10 seconds, followed by the full EA activation, which interrupted about 10 seconds later. When EA deactivated, The AP DISC parameter did not capture a button press. 

The pilot reported that he did not press the EA button at any time. 

The EA overhead panel and button were removed from the airplane and examined at the airframe manufacturer’s facility under the oversight of the FAA. The examination revealed that when pressed, the button would activate electrically before it travelled its full mechanical stroke (the electrical contacts would close when the button was only partially pressed). The button was found to be “slightly loose” when compared to an exemplar unit, though no obvious damage was noted. The exemplar button would consistently activate briefly when subjected to shock loading directed parallel to the axis of the button’s motion. 

Research and testing performed by the airplane manufacturer revealed two software programming defects in an exemplar integrated avionics system. The first was that during the EA activation sequence, there is a short window of time near the end of the 10 second warning period, during which the system would not respond to an AP DISC button press. If the button was pressed during the window, EA would not deactivate. If the button was pressed before or after the window, EA would deactivate. The precise duration of the window was not determined; however, it occurred between 8 and 10 seconds after initial activation of EA. 

The second defect was that the autopilot disconnect warning tone, which is designed to sound through the airplane’s audio system whenever the autopilot is disconnected, would not function if the AP DISC button was pressed at any time while EA is active. 

The airplane manufacturer advised that these 2 issues are scheduled to be addressed in a future software update.

20241017195337.an:
The pilot and two passengers completed an uneventful flight and refueled the airplane. They departed again, and while established in cruise flight, the engine gradually lost power. The pilot’s troubleshooting attempts were unsuccessful in restoring engine power, and the pilot performed a forced landing, which resulted in substantial damage to the left wing and fuselage.
Postaccident examination revealed that the air induction hose (scat duct) to the fuel servo was the incorrect part and was also damaged and degraded. The scat duct had several tears on the outside that were covered with orange sealant. The sealant was torn open in several places but appeared to have been previously covering tears in the scat duct. The scat duct’s internal metal wire was loose and had been rubbing/chafing on the inside of the airbox. The scat duct was able to collapse easily when light pressure was applied to the outside; the internal wiring shifted easily and allowed the scat duct to collapse. The collapsed duct would have restricted airflow to the engine and resulted in a loss of engine power.
During an annual inspection about 7 months before the accident, the lower cowl induction air scoop was rebonded to the engine cowling. The failed scat duct would have likely been removed and reinstalled to the airbox during this work, and the mechanic would have been able to assess its condition and recognize that it was not a manufacturer-approved part. The airplane’s maintenance logbooks did not document when the scat duct was originally installed or subsequently repaired.
20241017195337.fa:
On October 17, 2024, at 0947 central daylight time, a Piper PA-32R-301, N81481, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Van, Texas. The pilot and two passengers received minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
The pilot reported to the responding FAA inspector that he had just completed a flight to Terrell Municipal Airport (TRL), Terrell, Texas, where he received 60 gallons of fuel. He departed again and while established in cruise flight the engine began to gradually lose power, so he switched to the left fuel tank and partial power was restored. He then switched back to the right fuel tank, but the engine was unable to regain power. During the descent for an emergency landing, the pilot kept the landing gear and flaps retracted. The airplane collided with a wooden utility pole during landing, resulting in substantial damage to the left wing and fuselage.
The FAA inspector examined the airplane and found 30 to 35 gallons of 100LL aviation fuel in each of the fuel tanks. The fuel samples were free of water contamination. The engine remained attached to the firewall and did not exhibit signs of catastrophic failure.
Postaccident examination revealed that the air induction filter remained installed and appeared free of blockages. The air induction hose was impact separated from the fuel servo; this orange hose from the airbox to the fuel servo inlet adapter was an orange scat duct with no part numbers or identifying markings. The scat duct had several tears on the outside that were covered with an orange sealant. The sealant was ripped and torn in several places, but appeared to have been previously covering tears in the scat duct. The metal wire on the inside of the scat duct was loose and had been rubbing/chafing on the inside of the airbox. The scat duct was able to collapse easily when light pressure was applied to the outside of the scat duct; the internal wiring shifted easily, allowing the scat duct to collapse. There was no evidence of impact damage to the scat duct or the internal wiring. The orange scat duct was the incorrect part and should have been a double wall flexible air duct, part number 99849-08. 
The engine was removed from the airframe for a test run, which was completed with no anomalies noted. 
The airplane’s maintenance logbooks revealed that an annual inspection was completed on March 25, 2024, and another on August 1, 2024. During the March annual inspection, the lower cowl induction air scoop was rebonded to the engine cowling. The logbooks did not document when the scat duct was originally installed or subsequently repaired. 
On August 6, 2014, the FAA published a Special Airworthiness Information Bulletin (SAIB) CE-14-23 for certain Piper models, including the accident airplane model, regarding the air intake inlet hose (scat duct), specifically for structural deterioration and possible collapse of the air inlet hose. The air inlet hose may be between the air filter and the fuel injector, carburetor, or carburetor heat box depending on the airplane model. A collapsed hose reduces airflow to the engine and could result in a rough running engine or a loss of power. The SAIB recommended to inspect the inlet hose within the next 25 hours of time in service, and to verify that it is an approved Piper part and that it does not exhibit broken or loose cords on the external surface, loose or displaced supporting wire, or signs of wear, perforation, deterioration, or collapse. If an air inlet hose is observed exhibiting any of the conditions listed above or is not an approved Piper part, then the SAIB recommended replacement of the hose with an approved Piper part before the next flight.

20241019195345.an:
The pilot was approaching the destination airport following a short cross-country flight when he became incapacitated. The passenger reported that the pilot became unresponsive to her calling out to him. The passenger, who had no prior flight experience, reported that the pilot had already announced his intention to land on the airport’s common traffic advisory frequency (CTAF) and that she could see the airport when she took control of the airplane. Witnesses reported that she transmitted “emergency, emergency” on the CTAF. Although other pilots responded and offered assistance, she made no additional transmissions. 
FAA flight track data showed that after overflying the airport, the passenger made three unsuccessful landing attempts before landing on runway 5 on the fourth attempt. The last flight track data point showed the airplane about 250 ft southwest of the runway 05 threshold on a northeasterly track at a ground speed of 108 knots. The airplane impacted the runway nose first, collapsing the nose landing gear, and slid along the runway. A small fire subsequently developed near the forward portion of the airplane, and the lower forward fuselage sustained substantial damage. The pilot was transported to a local hospital, where he died two days later. 
Based on the available medical evidence, the pilot’s sudden incapacitation was likely due to in-flight cardiac arrest. The pilot had significant underlying heart disease, including coronary artery disease and heart damage from a previous heart attack. Toxicological testing identified no impairing substances. An autopsy was not performed. FAA records showed that the pilot had met the applicable BasicMed requirements for the flight.
20241019195345.fa:
On October 18, 2024, at 1826 eastern daylight time, a Cessna 150L airplane, N11519, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Gainesville, Georgia. The pilot became incapacitated while in flight and later died. The passenger sustained minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
Flight track data provided by the FAA indicated that the airplane departed Gwinnett County Airport (LZU), Lawrenceville, Georgia, at 1802 and proceeded toward Lee Gilmer Memorial Airport (GVL), Gainesville, Georgia. 
Shortly after the pilot announced his intention to land at GVL on the airport’s common traffic advisory frequency (CTAF), the passenger reported that the pilot became unresponsive. Witnesses reported that she transmitted “emergency, emergency” on the CTAF. Although other pilots responded and offered assistance, she made no additional transmissions. The passenger took control of the airplane, and made three unsuccessful landing attempts before landing on the fourth attempt at 1826 (see figure). The passenger, who had no previous flight experience, stated that she could see the airport when she took control of the airplane. The final flight track data point showed the airplane about 250 ft southwest of the runway 05 threshold on a northeasterly track at a ground speed of 108 knots.

Figure: FAA flight track data showing the passenger’s landing attempts at Lee Gilmer Memorial Airport (North is up).
Airport CCTV footage showed that the airplane landed on its nose landing gear, which collapsed, and the nose of the airplane impacted and slid along the runway. The pilot and passenger were subsequently met by witnesses who extinguished a small fire near the forward portion of the airplane. First responders later arrived and transported the pilot to a local hospital, where he died two days later. 
Examination of the airplane by an FAA inspector revealed substantial damage to the lower forward fuselage.
The pilot’s FAA medical certification file documented a medical history of diabetes, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol, all treated with medication. The pilot also had coronary artery disease and experienced a heart attack in 2009 that required quadruple coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery for severe multivessel disease. His medical history also included ischemic cardiomyopathy and atrial fibrillation treated with medication for heart rate control and stroke risk reduction.
The pilot completed a BasicMed course on March 22, 2022, and a BasicMed comprehensive medical examination checklist (CMEC) on March 24, 2022. The pilot subsequently completed another BasicMed course on March 4, 2024, and reported completing a BasicMed CMEC on March 3, 2024. The investigation found no evidence that the pilot completed the reported 2024 CMEC other than his self-report. The 2022 CMEC remained within its 48-month validity period as of the accident date.
When EMS first arrived, the pilot was in cardiac arrest. EMS initiated cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and transported the pilot to a local hospital. After arriving at the hospital, the pilot regained a pulse but remained critically ill following his cardiac arrest. The pilot died at the hospital two days after the accident. Hospital records characterized the pilot’s in-flight incapacitation event as a ventricular fibrillation cardiac arrest. An autopsy was not performed. 
Toxicological testing by the FAA Forensic Sciences Laboratory of the pilot’s hospital admission specimens detected metformin, carvedilol, and atorvastatin in blood. These medications are not typically impairing and were consistent with the pilot’s medications documented in the reviewed records. A hospital drug screen of a urine specimen collected on October 20, 2024, detected one drug class that could be attributed to medication administered to the pilot during his postaccident medical care.

The pilot reported that, after climbing to about 800 ft above ground level (agl), the engine suddenly stopped producing power. The pilot reported applying full carburetor heat and partial power was restored. The pilot then removed carburetor heat; again, the engine stopped producing power. The pilot applied full carburetor heat, and the engine regained partial power, but not enough to maintain altitude. The pilot made an emergency landing on a dirt road about three miles north of the airfield. During landing the left wing impacted brush and terrain along the road resulting in substantial damage to the left wing. 
A postaccident examination of the airframe and engine revealed no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures that would have precluded normal operation. Weather conditions at the time of the accident were conducive to carburetor icing at cruise power and serious carburetor icing at glide power. Although the pilot reported that he used the carburetor heat, it is likely that ice had already accumulated to the degree that the carburetor heat was insufficient to melt the ice and restore full engine power.
20241026195377.fa:
On October 24, 2024, about 1535 Hawaii-Aleutian standard time, a Cessna 150 airplane, N10495, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near Lanai, Hawaii. The pilot and passenger onboard were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. 
The pilot reported that, after climbing to about 800 ft agl, the engine suddenly stopped producing power. The pilot reported applying full carburetor heat and the engine began to make some power. The pilot then reduced carburetor heat and, again, the engine stopped producing power. Subsequently, the pilot applied full carburetor heat, and the engine began to produce some power; however, the engine was not producing enough power to maintain altitude. The pilot made an emergency landing on a dirt road about three miles north of the airfield. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the left wing. 
The automotive gas (Mogas) was drained from the carburetor bowl; no particulates or water was observed. Continuity was established between the throttle, mixture, and carburetor heat controls in the cockpit and the engine. 
The spark plug electrodes were inspected and found to have normal wear. The No. 4 cylinder spark plugs were observed to be white in color while the spark plugs from the other cylinders were observed to have a smoky dark gray appearance. Ignition was verified on all spark plugs. Thumb compression was observed on all cylinders. The cylinders were examined with a borescope and the No. 4 cylinder was observed to have light longitudinal scratches from top of ring travel to the bottom of the piston’s stroke. All cylinders were in serviceable condition. 
The airplane engine was started and idled within normal limits. The rpm was increased to 1,700 and the magnetos and carburetor heat both functioned normally and the engine ran smoothly. The rpm was increased to 2,400 and the engine ran a little rough; rpm was reduced to 2,000 rpm and the engine ran a little worse. The engine idled smoothly when warm at 700 rpm. The oil filter was removed; there were small flakes of metal observed in the oil filter media, but no glitter. The Marvel Schebler MA-3SPA 10-4894-1 carburetor was removed for further inspection. At the time of the accident the carburetor had 708.6 hours since overhaul. The carburetor was reported to be primarily run on unleaded Autogas. 
On December 5, 2024, the FAA and Marvel Schebler conducted a flow test and disassembled the carburetor. The flow test was slightly rich but within normal parameters. The carburetor was disassembled; a small amount of debris was noted on the internal filter but nothing likely to cause operational issues. 
On the day of the accident, at 1535, the weather reported at Lanai Airport (LNY), about 3 miles to the south of the accident site, included a temperature of 24°C and a dew point of 19°C. The calculated relative humidity at this temperature and dewpoint was 70%. Review of the icing probability chart contained within FAA Special Airworthiness Information Bulletin (CE-09-35) – Carburetor Icing Prevention, revealed the atmospheric conditions at the time of the accident were “conducive to serious icing at glide [idle] power.” 
The bulletin further stated that:
…pilots should be aware that carburetor icing doesn't just occur in freezing conditions, it can occur at temperatures well above freezing temperatures when there is visible moisture or high humidity. Icing can occur in the carburetor at temperatures above freezing because vaporization of fuel, combined with the expansion of air as it flows through the carburetor, (Venturi Effect) causes sudden cooling, sometimes by a significant amount within a fraction of a second. Carburetor ice can be detected by a drop in rpm in fixed pitch propeller airplanes and a drop in manifold pressure in constant speed propeller airplanes. In both types, usually there will be a roughness in engine operation.
According to FAA Advisory Circular 20-113, "To prevent accident due to induction system icing, the pilot should regularly use [carburetor] heat under conditions known to be conducive to atmospheric icing and be alert at all times for indications of icing in the fuel system." The circular recommended that, when operating in conditions where the relative humidity is greater than 50 percent, "…apply carburetor heat briefly immediately before takeoff, particularly with float type carburetors, to remove any ice which may have been accumulated during taxi and runup." It also stated, "Remain alert for indications of induction system icing during takeoff and climb-out, especially when the relative humidity is above 50 percent, or when visible moisture is present in the atmosphere." 
According to Transport Canada publication TP 10737 (Use of Automotive Gasoline [Mogas] in Aviation), Mogas is generally higher in volatility than Avgas and will thus absorb more heat from the mixing air when vaporizing, resulting in ice accumulation at higher ambient temperatures. It goes on to say that “the likelihood of carb icing while flying on Mogas is higher,” and advises that:
[a]lthough the severity of the carb icing and the methods to deal with it are similar for both Avgas and Mogas, its ONSET is likely to occur at HIGHER AMBIENT TEMPERATURES and LOWER HUMIDITY with Mogas. In other words, conditions under which a pilot may feel there is only a slight risk for carb icing on Avgas may in fact be ideal for the formation of ice while using more volatile Mogas. This will result in the need to select ‘carb heat on’ in less severe icing conditions and for a longer duration while using Mogas.

The pilot reported that he performed a flight control check before departing in his experimental, amateur-built airplane, and that the flight controls operated normally. During the initial climb, about 30 to 50 ft above ground level, the elevator control went slack. He could not regain elevator control and adjusted engine power in an attempt to regain control of the airplane’s pitch; however, the airplane descended and impacted the runway surface. The airplane skidded off the runway, the pilot egressed, and the airplane was destroyed by postimpact fire.
A postaccident examination of the airplane found that the top elevator control cable was not attached to the elevator horn. The securing bolt, nut, and cotter pin were not located. The lower elevator control cable remained attached via its bolt, but the securing nut and cotter pin were not located. A review of maintenance information about the airplane revealed that the airplane was originally assembled about three years before the accident, and had undergone several condition inspections, including one by a mechanic who was different than the owner/builder. The most recent condition inspection was performed by the owner/builder about nine months before the accident, and would have included inspection of all flight control surfaces. There was no logbook record of any recent maintenance to the elevator, nor did the pilot recall any. Based on the available information, it is likely that the elevator control cable was improperly secured during maintenance; however, when the maintenance occurred could not be determined.

After completing several training maneuvers during a helicopter instructional flight with a flight instructor, the student pilot was tasked to perform a simulated autorotation and to land on the runway. Data recovered from the helicopter’s avionics revealed that, during the simulated autorotation, the collective initially remained relatively steady during the descent, and the rotor rpm remained at or above 100%. 
Both the flight instructor and the student pilot reported that the touchdown on the runway was soft with no bounce or drift and good heading control as the helicopter entered the forward slide. However, as the helicopter continued to slide down the runway with decreasing groundspeed, it began to bounce laterally and shake violently with increasing severity before it came to a complete stop.
A postaccident examination of the helicopter revealed substantial damage on the tailboom assembly. Examination of the helicopter revealed no mechanical anomaly, and the flight instructor reported no mechanical malfunction or failure that would have precluded normal operation.
The data showed also that, as the helicopter descended through about 30 ft above ground level (agl), the collective began to increase sharply, and the rotor rpm began to drop below 100%. After touchdown on the runway, the collective continued to be increased, resulting in the rotor rpm continuing to decline. This increase in collective control was inconsistent with helicopter’s flight manual, which stated that the collective should be lowered after landing.
Although the data showed that the helicopter’s horizontal speed, rate of descent, attitude, and vertical acceleration at touchdown were consistent with the parameters for a power-off landing, the data also showed that, as the helicopter subsequently slid along the runway, rapid oscillations in helicopter pitch, roll, and yaw developed. Divergent oscillations in vertical, lateral, and longitudinal accelerations also occurred, the peak of which was about 3.6 G in the vertical direction when the rotor system had slowed to about 45%. 
Further review of the data determined that, as the rotor slowed to about 40%, the rotor vibration frequency started to match with the oscillation frequencies of the helicopter’s pitch and roll angles and the lateral, longitudinal, and vertical accelerations as it slid along the runway. It is likely that a resonance developed between the vibrations of the slow-turning rotor system and the vibrations of airframe, resulting in increasing loads on the airframe that exceeded the airframe structural limitations and damaged the tailboom. Had the collective been lowered after touchdown per the rotorcraft flight manual’s procedure, it is unlikely that resonance would have occurred.
20241029195393.fa:
On August 23, 2024, about 1130 eastern standard time, a Bell Textron Canada 505 helicopter, N945TC, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Marianna, Florida. The student pilot and the flight instructor were uninjured. The helicopter was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulation Part 91 instructional flight.
ADS-B data showed that the helicopter departed Dothan Regional Airport (DHN), Dothan, Alabama, flew to the Marianna Municipal Airport (MAI), Marianna, Florida, then performed several circuits in the traffic pattern at MAI. According to the flight instructor and the student pilot, the student pilot then performed a practice autorotation to touchdown on the runway. 
The flight instructor reported that the student pilot initiated the landing flare about 80 ft agl with a “good nose-up pitch to bleed airspeed without any aggressive rotor buildup.” The flight instructor stated that, as the helicopter began to settle to about 10 to 15 ft agl, the student pilot applied increased collective with some forward nose cyclic for a level landing at a touchdown speed of about 20 to 25 kts. Both the flight instructor and the student pilot reported that the landing on the runway was soft with no bounce or drift and good heading control as it entered the slide. As the helicopter continued to slide down the runway with decreasing groundspeed, it began to bounce laterally and shake “violently” with increasing severity before it came to a complete stop. A postaccident examination of the helicopter revealed that the tailboom doublers at the attachment point to the truss assembly were deformed.
The helicopter was equipped with an avionics suite that recorded various helicopter position, engine, flight control, attitude, and acceleration parameters. The system automatically adjusted the vertical acceleration recorded values to remove the standard 1G of gravity. The data revealed that, just before the helicopter’s IDLE/FLY switch was switched to the idle position for the simulated autorotation, the helicopter was at an altitude of about 925 ft agl in a slightly nose-down attitude with a slight left bank and an airspeed of about 75 kts. The collective was initially positioned at 33%, the rotor rpm and power turbine speed (NP) were both at 104%, and the gas generator speed (NG) was at approximately 91%. The collective was then lowered to 10%, resulting in a decrease in NG to 82%, while the rotor rpm and NP both remained constant at 104%. During this transition, helicopter’s pitch attitude varied between 2° and 5° nose down, and its airspeed increased to 80 kts. 
The IDLE/FLY switch was then put into the IDLE position for the simulated autorotation, and the engine responded by going to idle. The helicopter’s pitch was increased, and its airspeed slowed to about 70 kts, which was consistent with the Bell 505 Rotorcraft Flight Manual’s recommended speed for best glide. The helicopter continued to operate near 70 kts as it began a descent toward the runway. 
As the helicopter descended through about 125 ft agl, its pitch angle leveled off. When the helicopter was about 60 ft agl, its pitch angle increased to about 20° nose up, and the helicopter’s vertical descent rate decreased from about 1,600 ft per minute (fpm) to about 800 fpm. 
During the flare, the rotor rpm was about 105% and remained stable above 100%, and the collective remained relatively unchanged between 12% and 16% during most of the descent toward the ground. When the helicopter was approximately 30 ft agl, the collective began to increase sharply to 38%, and the rotor rpm began to drop below 100%. 
The data showed that, as the helicopter touched down on the runway, the collective continued to be increased, and the rotor rpm decreased to about 67%. Shortly after touchdown, rapid oscillations in helicopter pitch, roll, and yaw developed, and several divergent oscillations in the vertical, lateral, and longitudinal accelerations occurred. These oscillations continued for several seconds, with a peak vertical acceleration of 3.631 Gs, a peak lateral acceleration of 2.718 Gs, and a peak longitudinal acceleration of -2.165 Gs. At the time the peak vertical and lateral accelerations were recorded, the rotor rpm was about 45%, and the peak longitudinal acceleration occurred when the rotor rpm was about 41%. 
According to the helicopter manufacturer’s review of the data, the helicopter’s horizontal speed, rate of descent, attitude, and vertical acceleration at touchdown were consistent with the parameters for a power-off landing. The manufacturer determined that the subsequent divergent oscillations of the vertical, lateral, and longitudinal accelerations, as well as the oscillation frequencies of the helicopter’s pitch and roll angles, closely matched the helicopter’s rotor vibration frequency at the reduced rotor rpm. 
A review of the Bell 505 Rotorcraft Flight Manual revealed the procedure for an in-flight engine failure (requiring an autorotation) prescribed maintaining heading and attitude while lowering the collective to maintain the required 90% to 111% rotor rpm. The procedure also stated that, after landing, the collective should be lowered smoothly. 
A review of the operator’s flight training syllabus revealed that, for a standard autorotation to a touchdown, the standard was to maintain rotor speed within the rotorcraft flight manual-specified limits throughout the descent and flare.

The flight instructor stated that after departure, the airplane’s acceleration felt sluggish. Despite troubleshooting, the airplane would not climb as expected and he decided to return to the airport. After realizing that the airplane would not make it back to the runway, he made an off-airport landing on soft desert terrain. The airplane landed hard and erupted into flames. 

A review of the recorded engine monitor data did not identify an abrupt loss of manifold pressure, fuel flow, oil pressure, or combustion from an individual cylinder during the takeoff or flight. The engine did not attain its rated speed despite the manifold pressure remaining as expected for takeoff, and the airplane accelerated slowly during the takeoff roll. The data were consistent with reduced available power or thrust during the takeoff and initial climb. 

The recorded data alone could not determine whether the reduced performance resulted from the engine fuel-metering or mixture system, the ignition system, or the propeller system. The postaccident examination revealed no evidence of mechanical malfunction or failures; however, numerous systems were unable to be examined due to excessive damage from the postaccident fire. Therefore, the reason for the reduction of power could not be determined.
20241029195404.fa:
HISTORY OF FLIGHTOn October 27, 2024, about 1712 mountain standard time, a Cirrus Design Corp. SR20 airplane, N27WF, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near St. George, Utah. The flight instructor, student pilot, and passenger were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight.

The flight instructor stated that the purpose of the flight was to drop the passenger off in Provo, Utah, while also providing the owner/student with familiarization experience in the airplane. The flight instructor reported that, during the run-up, he noticed the left magneto was running rough with about a 150-rpm drop. Assuming spark plug fouling, he leaned the mixture for several minutes and then repeated the magneto check, which showed normal operation. Thereafter, they departed from runway 19, and the flight instructor noted that the airplane’s acceleration felt sluggish, which he attributed to the added weight. He stated that the airplane climbed normally to about 200 ft above ground level before it would no longer accelerate, although the engine sounded normal.

The flight instructor stated that he cycled the throttle, adjusted the mixture, and confirmed that the flaps were at 50 percent. He reported that, despite those actions, the airplane did not accelerate. With rising terrain ahead, he banked left toward the airport. After realizing that the airplane would not make it back to the runway, he maintained a controlled descent to avoid a stall. During the off-airport landing on soft desert terrain, he flared aggressively to reduce ground speed. The left wing dropped and the airplane landed hard, which resulted in separation of the landing gear. The airplane then skidded and rotated about 180° to 270° before it came to rest upright. The occupants exited the airplane, and a fire ensued shortly thereafter. The airplane came to rest about 5 miles south of the airport.

According to the flight instructor, the engine and propeller appeared and sounded normal during the accident flight but did not produce the expected thrust. He recalled that the boost pump was on, but he could not remember which fuel tank was selected because he had followed the checklist and switched tanks after the run-up. He stated that the airbags did not deploy. AIRCRAFT INFORMATIONThe airplane was equipped with a four-cylinder, air-cooled, direct-drive, horizontally opposed, fuel-injected engine, rated at 215 horsepower at 2,700 rpm.

A review of the maintenance records revealed that the airplane was maintained under the Cirrus 400-hour progressive inspection program until 2023. An entry dated January 29, 2024, stated that the airplane was no longer maintained under the Cirrus 400-hour progressive inspection program and that a 100-hour/annual inspection had been completed at an airframe total time of 1,509.7 hours. 

The flight instructor reported that the airplane had been purchased about 5 months before the accident. The flight instructor estimated that the airplane was about 230 pounds below maximum gross weight. AIRPORT INFORMATIONThe airplane was equipped with a four-cylinder, air-cooled, direct-drive, horizontally opposed, fuel-injected engine, rated at 215 horsepower at 2,700 rpm.

A review of the maintenance records revealed that the airplane was maintained under the Cirrus 400-hour progressive inspection program until 2023. An entry dated January 29, 2024, stated that the airplane was no longer maintained under the Cirrus 400-hour progressive inspection program and that a 100-hour/annual inspection had been completed at an airframe total time of 1,509.7 hours. 

The flight instructor reported that the airplane had been purchased about 5 months before the accident. The flight instructor estimated that the airplane was about 230 pounds below maximum gross weight. TESTS AND RESEARCHEngine Data Recorder

The airplane was equipped with an Appareo RDM-300 recoverable data module. The recovered file contained about 22 minutes of data, from 1651:12 to 1713:34, and included engine rpm, manifold pressure, fuel flow, calculated percent power, oil pressure and temperature, individual cylinder exhaust gas temperature (EGT) and cylinder head temperature (CHT), and airplane performance parameters.

At 1654:00, the engine started and operated for about 6 minutes and 42 seconds. During a likely ground run-up, the engine speed increased to a maximum of 2,267 rpm. At 1700:42, the engine stopped. The data then recorded several short engine-start attempts before the engine restarted at 1704:45. During a second ground run-up, the engine speed increased to a maximum of 2,475 rpm, decreased to about 600 rpm, and then returned to about 2,200 rpm.

At 1708:31, the manifold pressure increased to about 27 inHg, consistent with the application of takeoff power. The fuel flow increased to about 9 gph, and the engine speed increased to about 2,300 rpm. The engine speed increased gradually as the airplane accelerated and first exceeded 2,500 rpm about 36 seconds later. The airplane reached 70 knots indicated airspeed about 49 seconds after the increase in manifold pressure. The maximum recorded engine speed was 2,636 rpm, slightly below the engine’s rated speed of 2,700 rpm.

After the engine speed exceeded 2,500 rpm, the manifold pressure remained between 26.8 and 27.0 inHg, the fuel flow remained between 9.2 and 9.7 gph, and the calculated percent power remained between 82% and 87%. The recorded engine parameters remained generally stable until about 1712:19, when the manifold pressure, fuel flow, and engine speed decreased during the final seconds of the accident sequence.

A review of the recorded data did not identify an abrupt loss of manifold pressure, fuel flow, oil pressure, or combustion from an individual cylinder during the takeoff or flight. The engine did not attain its rated speed despite the manifold pressure remaining near 27 inHG, and the airplane accelerated slowly during the takeoff roll. The data was consistent with reduced available power or thrust during the takeoff and initial climb.

Cirrus provided four previous flight recordings from October 21 and October 25, 2024. Two of the previous departures were from St. George Regional Airport and two were from Provo Municipal Airport.

During the four previous takeoffs, the engine speed exceeded 2,600 rpm within 4 to 6 seconds after the initial increase in manifold pressure and then stabilized near 2,700 rpm. The manifold pressure stabilized between about 25.3 and 27.0 inHg, and the fuel flow stabilized between about 13.0 and 19.4 gph. The airplane accelerated to 70 knots indicated airspeed within 17 to 23 seconds. At 60 seconds after the application of takeoff power, the altitude had increased between about 219 and 323 ft above the runway elevation.

During comparable portions of the two previous St. George takeoffs, the average engine speeds were about 2,703 and 2,710 rpm, and the average fuel flows were about 17.3 and 19.4 gph. During the accident takeoff, the average engine speed was about 2,461 rpm and the average fuel flow was about 9.2 gph. The accident-flight EGT values averaged between about 1,457°F and 1,516°F, compared with about 1,264°F to 1,395°F during the previous St. George takeoffs. The CHT values during the accident takeoff were slightly higher than during the previous takeoffs but remained stable.

Examination

The postaccident examination revealed that the engine remained attached to the airframe by the engine mount and had sustained severe thermal damage from the postimpact fire. The accessory case housing and attached accessories, including the magnetos, fuel pump, vacuum pump, and oil filter, had been consumed by fire. 

Rotation of the crankshaft was precluded by thermal damage to the engine case and cylinders. The combustion chambers were examined through the spark plug holes with a lighted borescope. The combustion chambers and bottom spark plug electrodes remained mechanically undamaged, and there was no evidence of foreign object ingestion. The valves were intact and undamaged, and there was no evidence of valve-to-piston contact.

Additional borescope examination through holes drilled in the top of the engine case allowed visualization of the connecting rods, crankshaft, and cam lobes. Investigators reported no evidence of lubrication deprivation or contamination. The crankshaft and connecting rods were free of heat distress. The roller tappet camshaft was intact, and each cam lobe exhibited its characteristic elliptical shape. The accessory gears, including the crankshaft gear, bolt, and dowel, were intact and exhibited no evidence of a preimpact malfunction.

A majority of the fuel system was consumed by fire and could not be functionally examined.

Shortly after takeoff, as the airplane was climbing through 300 ft above ground level, the engine misfired, then suddenly stopped producing power. Unable to troubleshoot due to the low altitude, the pilot lowered the nose and attempted a forced landing on the remaining runway. The airplane landed hard, collapsing the landing gear and damaging the wings and airframe. 
Postaccident examination of the airplane did not reveal any engine anomalies; however, an examination of the fuel system revealed the fuel gascolator was installed partially outside of the engine compartment, exposing it to the air slipstream. The gascolator exhibited features consistent with a fuel leak. The gascolator bowl was not completely secure to the upper portion of the gascolator and it leaked fuel when touched by hand. 
The most recent engine maintenance was completed about 10 days before the accident and, although the fuel gascolator gasket was not mentioned in the logbook entry, a fuel system inspection was documented. The condition of the gasket would have warranted replacement. 
The gascolator bowl gasket was stiff and cracked, which likely allowed fuel to leak out during the flight, starving the engine of fuel. The circumstances of the accident are consistent with a total loss of engine power due to fuel starvation, which resulted in a loss of engine power and hard landing.

On October 17, 2024, at 1515 eastern daylight time, an experimental amateur-built Zenith Zodiac 601HDS airplane, N511JG, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Altoona, Pennsylvania. The private pilot was not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
The private pilot reported that there were no irregularities noted with the airplane during the preflight inspection, engine run-up, or taxi before departing from runway 3 at Altoona/Blair County Airport (AOO), Altoona, Pennsylvania. The pilot intended to remain in the airport traffic pattern; however, during the initial climb, when the airplane was climbing through 300 ft above ground level, the engine started to “misfire,” then immediately stopped producing power. Unable to troubleshoot due to the low altitude, the pilot lowered the nose and attempted a forced landing on the remaining runway.
The airplane landed hard and the landing gear collapsed, which resulted in the wings and airframe buckling. The airplane then skidded to a stop on the side of the runway. 
Examination of the airplane revealed signatures to the propeller that were consistent with a lack of rotation during the impact; the engine was intact. Engine crankshaft and valvetrain continuity was established and compression was attained on each cylinder. Both magnetos produced spark at each of the posts. A subsequent examination of the fuel system revealed 10 gallons of fuel on board. In addition, the fuel gascolator was installed partially outside of the engine compartment, exposing it to the air slipstream. The gascolator exhibited features consistent with a fuel leak. The gascolator bowl was not completely secure to the upper portion of the gascolator and it would leak fuel when lightly touched by hand. The gascolator was opened and the gasket at the top of the bowl was found to be stiff and cracked. 
A review of maintenance records documented an annual condition inspection had been completed about 10 days before the accident. The logbook entry did not document any maintenance or inspection to the gascolator specifically, but the fuel system inspection was documented and tested, yielding no leaks.

20241030195417.an:
After landing, the airplane was refueled, and six passengers boarded. During the airplane’s approximately 15-minute ground stop, a witness observed that heavy, wet snow was falling. Before taxi, the pilot used a foam brush to remove snow from the airplane. The witness further observed snow contamination on an outboard wing section after the pilot finished brushing the airplane. 
Heavy snowfall continued as the airplane taxied but diminished by the time the airplane began its takeoff roll. During rotation, the airplane became airborne briefly before the left wing dropped and struck terrain.
According to the airplane’s pilot’s operating handbook (POH), even small accumulations of snow, frost, or ice must be removed from the wings, tail, and control surfaces during the preflight inspection. The POH also called for anti-icing fluid shortly before takeoff from a snow-covered runway. The risks of snow and ice accumulation were also addressed in a 2018 service letter (SL) from the airplane manufacturer, which stated that takeoffs with snow or ice adhering to the wings should not be attempted because such contamination could drastically affect performance due to reduced aerodynamic lift and increased drag resulting from disturbed airflow. The SL also provided recommendations for ground deicing and anti-icing procedures and emphasized the need for a pre-takeoff contamination inspection.
The left wing drop shortly after liftoff was consistent with an aerodynamic stall. The stall was likely the result of snow contamination that remained on the wing after the pilot brushed the airplane; the amount of snow on the wing also likely increased as snow continued to fall during taxi. The contamination reduced aerodynamic lift and increased drag, which resulted in a loss of control shortly after takeoff. Because snow continued to fall during taxi, the lack of anti-icing fluid also left the cleaned surfaces exposed to renewed accumulation. Although Type I fluid was available for deicing, the manufacturer cautioned that it would provide inadequate anti-icing protection during snowfall unless takeoff followed deicing almost immediately. The other fluid reportedly available, Type IV, was unsuitable for this airplane. The absence of preimpact mechanical failures or malfunctions further supported an aerodynamic, rather than mechanical, explanation for the loss of control. A review of two previous accidents involving the same airplane type and similar circumstances revealed similar left-wing drops shortly after liftoff. 
The pilot’s reported rotation speed of 85 knots was slightly below the charted rotation speed of about 87 knots for the airplane’s reported takeoff weight. Rotating early likely further reduced the airplane’s safety margin during liftoff.

On October 29, 2024, about 1645 mountain daylight time, a Daher TBM 700N (marketed as the TBM 850) airplane, N885CA, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Pinedale, Wyoming. The pilot and five passengers sustained minor injuries, and one passenger sustained serious injuries. The flight was conducted under Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 as a personal flight.
According to a witness at Ralph Wenz Field Airport (PNA), Pinedale, Wyoming, the airplane landed and was refueled. About 40 gallons of fuel were added to each tank, and six passengers boarded the airplane during the stop. He noted that heavy, wet snow fell during the airplane’s time on the ground. The airplane was on the ground for about 15 minutes. Before taxi, the pilot used a foam brush to remove snow from the airplane. The witness observed snow contamination on an outboard wing section after the pilot finished brushing the airplane. The airport manager reported that he informed the pilot about the availability of Type I and Type IV deicing and anti-icing fluids at the airport prior to the accident flight, which the pilot declined. 
The heavy snowfall continued as the airplane taxied but became light when the airplane began its takeoff roll on runway 29. During rotation, the airplane became airborne briefly before the left wing dropped and struck terrain. The airplane’s left wing and fuselage sustained substantial damage. The pilot reported the runway condition as “wet and snow-wet.”
Postaccident examination of the airframe revealed no evidence of preimpact mechanical failures or malfunctions that would have precluded normal operation. Flight control continuity was confirmed. The left aileron had separated during the accident sequence, but its outboard portion remained attached to the aileron linkage and moved appropriately when establishing continuity with the control columns. The flaps measured near the takeoff setting of 10°.
The pilot reported a takeoff gross weight of about 6,939 pounds, which was below the maximum takeoff weight of 7,394 pounds. The airplane’s estimated center of gravity was within limits. 
The pilot stated that he used a rotation speed of 85 knots. The POH takeoff performance chart indicated a rotation speed of about 87 knots for the reported takeoff weight. About 2,400 ft down the runway, the airplane started to turn left, and impact markings were consistent with the left wing striking terrain beyond the runway’s edge. The airplane continued on a heading about 20° left of the runway heading until it came to rest on a dirt berm about 300 ft from the runway edge. Numerous small airplane fragments were distributed along the debris path from the initial left-wing impact to the main wreckage.
According to the POH, even small accumulations of frost, ice, or snow must be removed from the wings, tail, and control surfaces during the preflight inspection. For takeoff from a runway covered with melting or untamped snow, the POH directs pilots to apply anti-icing fluid to the wings, stabilizers, movable surfaces, and landing gear wells shortly before takeoff. For an icy or tamped-snow runway, it directs application to the wings, stabilizers, and movable surfaces. A service letter (SL) from the airplane manufacturer stated that takeoffs with snow or ice adhering to the wings should not be attempted because such contamination could drastically affect performance due to reduced aerodynamic lift and increased drag resulting from disturbed airflow. The SL described mechanical removal and one- and two-step ground deicing and anti-icing procedures and called for a pre-takeoff contamination inspection. The airport manager reported that Type I and Type IV fluids were available on the day of the accident. The SL identified Type I fluid for deicing and Type III fluid for anti-icing, but cautioned that Type I provides inadequate anti-icing protection during snowfall unless takeoff follows deicing almost immediately. It advised against using Type II or Type IV fluid on the TBM 700 because of its low rotation speed. 
The pilot stated that ensuring all hard surfaces, including the ramp, taxiway, and runway, were completely plowed before engine start might have prevented the accident. The POH stated that the airplane’s maximum occupancy was limited by the installed approved seating configuration but could not exceed six people, including the pilot. The pilot and six passengers were aboard the airplane. 
A review of two National Transportation Safety Board accident reports involving the same airplane type revealed similar accidents after the pilots failed to ensure ice and snow had been removed from the airplane’s surfaces before takeoff. In CEN12LA153, the left wing dropped just after the airplane became airborne during takeoff. Similarly, in the CEN24FA046 report, a witness reported that the takeoff appeared to be normal before the left wing dropped shortly after rotation. The airplane manufacturer stated that the left wing would typically stall first, which was expected behavior for a conventional single-engine airplane equipped with a clockwise-turning propeller. The accident airplane had a weather radar pod installed on the left wing; however, manufacturer flight tests conducted without the pod also resulted in the left wing stalling first.

The student pilot was on the second leg of a long visual flight rules cross-country flight. The pilot departed shortly after the end of civil twilight and on a night where no lunar illumination was present. The pilot had not filed a flight plan and there was no evidence that he had obtained an official weather briefing from a source that would have logged that contact. After departure, the pilot flew over a town that contained significant cultural lighting and highway, flying parallel to a road for about 1 mile. He then turned away from the town and roughly toward the destination airport, over a sparsely populated area covered with dense forest and rising terrain. 
The dark night, in addition to the generally cloudy conditions and limited ground lighting along the flight path, would have made it difficult for the pilot to visually recognize the rising terrain. As the pilot continued toward this area of diminished visual reference, he encountered a band of light rain showers, which in addition to further restricting visibility, had the potential for updrafts and associated turbulence. Given these conditions, it is likely that the pilot was flying in instrument meteorological conditions (IMC) for the last 4 minutes of the flight. Postaccident examination of the wreckage at the accident site revealed no evidence of any preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures of the airframe or engine. The relatively straight flight path for the final portion of the flight that was observed via ADS-B, the length of the wreckage path at the accident site, and the damage observed to trees along that wreckage path, were all consistent with controlled flight into terrain. 
The results of postaccident toxicological testing indicated that the pilot had used the prescription medication lamotrigine. While it is possible that his cognitive and psychomotor performance might have been impaired by the effects of the medication, no more-specific conclusion about pilot impairment can be drawn from the reviewed medical evidence alone. Based on the available information, the student pilot’s decision to continue the long cross-country flight at night, without obtaining a preflight weather briefing or having an apparent awareness of approaching precipitation, and without filing a flight plan, was indicative of poor judgement.
