The pilot stated that shortly after takeoff the engine made a popping noise with a noticeable loss of engine thrust. The rpm gauge indicated “0” but the propeller continued to rotate. The pilot declared a MAYDAY and made a forced landing in the ocean. Postaccident examination of the engine revealed that the crankshaft gear bolt was about 1/8th inch out from being seated on the crankshaft gear. The crankshaft gear bolt head was rounded, and the bottom threads of the bolt were damaged. The crankshaft gear was removed, and the alignment dowel was found sheared. Four teeth were also sheared from the oil adapter idler gear. Metallurgical examination of the fractured components determined they had fractured from shear overstress. 
Per the engine maintenance log, at the last annual inspection (about 6 months prior to the accident), the engine had had accrued about 650 hours since it was overhauled. There were no entries in the maintenance records to indicate the crankshaft bolt had been removed, inspected, or modified since the engine had been overhauled. Based on the available information it is likely that when the engine was overhauled, the crankshaft gear bolt was not properly seated against the crankshaft gear, which resulted in the crankshaft gear eventually disengaging from the accessory gears leading to a total loss of engine power.
20250603200256.fa:
On June 1, 2025, at 1028 eastern daylight time, a Piper PA32-300 airplane, N2242Z, was involved in an accident near Branford, Connecticut. The private pilot/owner and the passenger were not injured. The flight was conducted as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
The pilot departed from Bridgeport/Sikorsky Airport (BDR), Bridgeport, Connecticut, about 1014, and was en route to Block Island State Airport (BID), Block Island, Rhode Island. The pilot stated that all engine indications were normal as he climbed and leveled off at 3,000 ft mean sea level (msl) over Long Island Sound. Shortly after, the engine made a popping noise “similar to a backfire” with a noticeable loss of engine thrust. The pilot noted the engine rpm gauge went to “0” but the propeller continued to rotate. He declared a MAYDAY and made a forced landing in the water south of Branford, Connecticut.
The airplane was equipped with a Garmin G3X, which recorded flight and engine data. Review of data obtained from that device revealed that after takeoff, the airplane was headed eastbound at an airspeed of about 120 knots, at 3,000 ft msl. At 1023, the engine speed dropped from 2,390 rpm to 520 rpm, and to 0 rpm 2 seconds later. The engine speed remained 0 rpm for the rest of the flight. All the other engine parameters corresponded to the loss of engine power consecutively, including a drop of exhaust gas temperature, oil pressure, and fuel flow rate. The last recorded data point was at 1028, just before the airplane landed in the water.
The airplane wreckage was recovered and taken to a secure facility for further examination. Both wings had been removed, and substantial damage was observed on the lower fuselage. The engine and its two-blade propeller remained securely attached to the airframe. Evidence of corrosion was noted from exposure to saltwater. The rocker box covers were removed, and no anomalies were noted. The crankshaft was rotated when force was applied to the propeller. Thumb compressions were established on all cylinders, but valve action movement was not observed on any of the cylinders. 
The engine was removed from the airframe to facilitate further examination. The accessory section of the engine was removed, and the crankshaft gear bolt was found about 1/8th inch out from the seated position. The safety lock plate washer was installed. The crankshaft gear bolt head was rounded. The crankshaft gear bolt was removed, and the bottom threads of the bolt were damaged. The crankshaft gear was removed, and the alignment dowel was sheared. Four teeth were sheared from the oil adapter idler gear and found in the oil sump. Per Lycoming, the head of the crankshaft gear bolt appeared to be marked 2247, which indicated the bolt was a Lycoming STD-2247, the applicable crankshaft gear bolt for this engine. 
The oil pump idler gear, remnants of four teeth from the oil pump idler gear, the oil pump drive shaft, and the crankshaft gear with crankshaft gear bolt, and the crankshaft alignment dowel pin were examined by the NTSB Materials Laboratory. The broken components from the engine, the crankshaft alignment dowel pin, and four teeth from the oil pump idler gear were determined to have fractured from shear overstress. All the other components exhibited damage consistent with rotational wear or contact damage with adjacent components. There were no features suggesting pre-existing damage in the fractured components. 
The electronic tachometer was damaged from saltwater exposure, and a reading was not attainable. A review of the engine maintenance records revealed the engine was last overhauled on August 27, 2018. The last annual inspection prior to the accident was completed on January 16, 2025, and the engine had accrued 648.9 hours since overhaul. There were no entries in the records to indicate that the crankshaft gear bolt had been removed/inspected/modified since the engine had been overhauled.
According to the Textron Lycoming Direct Drive Overhaul Manual, Section 7-65, Crankshaft Gear; "Assemble the gear to the crankshaft using both a new lockplate and bolt. The correct bolt, lockplate and dowel for each gear are shown in Table 7-4. Tighten the bolt to 125 inch lbs. torque, then with a hammer and brass drift, tap lightly around the pilot flange of the gear and listen for sharp solid sounds from the hammer blows that would indicate that the gear is seated against the crankshaft. As a check on seating against the crankshaft, attempt to insert a pointed .001 inch thick feeler gage or shim stock between the gear and crankshaft at each of the three scallops. The .001 feeler gage, or any smaller feeler gage, must fit between the two surfaces at any location. (.001 feeler gage is used as an indicator, however there must be no clearance between crankshaft and gear.) Retighten the gear attaching bolt to the proper torque. Tighten the 5/16 inch bolt to 204 inch-pound torque or the 1/2 inch bolt to 660 inch-pound torque. Measure the clearance between the O.D. of the gear flange and the pilot I.D. of the crankshaft. There should not be more than .0005 inch clearance at any point. Bend the lockplate against the bolt head."
On January 23, 2003, Lycoming issued a mandatory service bulletin (SB475C) for crankshaft gear modification and assembly procedures that in part stated, "Damage to the crankshaft gear and the counterbored recess in the rear of the crankshaft, as well as badly worn or broken gear alignment dowels are the result of improper assembly techniques or the reuse of worn or damaged parts during reassembly. Since a failure of the gear or the gear attaching parts would result in complete engine stoppage, the proper inspection and reassembly of these parts is very important."
Step 6 of the procedures described the assembly of the gear to the crankshaft using a new lockplate and bolt, "Assemble the gear to the crankshaft using both a new lockplate and bolt. Refer to Figure 6. The correct bolt, lockplate and dowel for each gear are shown in Table 2. Tighten the bolt to 125 in.-lbs. torque, then with a hammer and brass drift, tap lightly around the pilot flange of the gear and listen for sharp solid sounds from the hammer blows that would indicate that the gear is seated against the crankshaft. As a check on the seating against the crankshaft, attempt to insert a pointed .001 inch thick feeler gage or shim stock between the gear and crankshaft at each of the three scallops. The .001 feeler gage, or any smaller feeler gage, must NOT fit between the two surfaces at any location. (.001 feeler gage is used as an indicator, however, there must be no clearance between crankshaft and gear.) Retighten the gear attaching bolt to the proper torque. Tighten the 5/16 inch bolt to 204 in.-lbs. torque or the 1 1/2 inch bolt to 660 in.-lbs. torque. Measure the clearance between the O.D. of the gear flange and the pilot I.D. of the crankshaft. There should not be more than .0005 inch clearance at any point."
On September 12, 2016, Lycoming issued supplement No. 1 to the mandatory service bulletin that provided an alternate method of compliance to Service Bulletin No. 475C if the crankshaft gear was replaced rather than modified.

20250604200259.an:
The pilot and two passengers were on a multi-leg cross-country flight under instrument flight rules. After refueling the airplane fully, they departed on the accident flight and flew to an intermediate airport where the pilot performed a practice instrument approach. After landing the airplane and departing again, they flew toward the destination airport, where the pilot planned to perform another practice instrument approach. About 1-mile from the final approach fix, and while flying over the ocean, the airplane’s engine suddenly lost power. The pilot had his passenger inform air traffic control of the emergency before ditching the airplane into the water about 5 miles offshore. All three occupants incurred minor injuries and were rescued after the accident. The airplane was not recovered and presumed substantially damaged. 
Review of ADS-B data for the flight revealed that the airplane had been aloft for less than 2.5 hours since last being fueled to its full capacity of 38 gallons. According to the airplane’s Pilot Operating Handbook, at cruise power settings the airplane’s estimated consumption ranged from 8.0 to 9.0 gallons per hour. Accounting for fuel consumed during taxi, takeoff, climb, and descent, the total fuel consumption for the flight was estimated to be between 20 and 23 gallons. This suggests that about 15 to 18 gallons of usable fuel remained at the time of the accident.
The weather conditions reported at the destination airport included a calculated relative humidity of 40% percent. Review of the icing probability chart contained within Federal Aviation Administration Special Airworthiness Information Bulletin CE-09-35 revealed the atmospheric conditions at the time of the accident were conducive to serious carburetor icing at glide power. Because the airplane was not recovered, and the wreckage could not be examined, the reason for the loss of engine power could not be determined.

20250604200265.an:
The pilot of the multi-engine airplane reported that he was completing a cross-country flight and was nearing the next fuel stop at the time of the accident. The pilot reported that only the main fuel tanks were used for the flight due to a fuel leak in the auxiliary fuel tanks. While nearing the airport, the pilot encountered unexpected weather and had to divert several times around the weather. After he diverted around the patches of weather and on approach to the airport, he reported entering a rainstorm with heavy precipitation. He then began a climbing turn to exit the weather; during the climb, the left engine lost power. As he attempted to regain engine power of the left engine, which included turning on the carburetor heat, the right engine began to lose power, after which the airplane could no longer maintain altitude. The pilot then determined that a forced landing was required, and he ditched the airplane in a river. Postaccident examination of the airplane revealed that it had sustained substantial damage to the fuselage and empennage. 
The examination of the wreckage revealed several maintenance problems, such as the right engine’s carburetor leaking from the gasket, the right engine’s carburetor float valve missing the attach bracket, and the left engine’s fuel strainer housing having severe corrosion. Any of these items could have contributed to a loss of power in a particular engine; however, since the loss of power from both engines occurred within a short period of time, it is unlikely that these maintenance issues would have resulted in a near simultaneous loss of engine power.
Postaccident examination of the airframe’s fuel system revealed that there was no fuel remaining in the left main fuel tank and approximately 4 gallons remained in the right main fuel tank. No documentation could be found in the airplane’s operator’s handbook or type certificate data sheet that indicated how much fuel was unusable in each fuel tank. An airplane of similar design on the same type certificate data sheet indicated that its unusable fuel was 1.7 gallons per fuel tank. If the accident airplane’s fuel system had a similar unusable amount of fuel, that would indicate the airplane only had about 2.3 gallons of usable fuel remaining. 
A review of the weather conditions at the time of the accident revealed that it was conducive to serious carburetor icing at glide engine power settings. At the time of the loss of power, the pilot had was approaching his next fuel stop and would have likely been at a low power setting, during that approach. Additionally, the pilot entered a rainstorm, which would increase the amount of moisture that was in the air, increasing the chances of carburetor ice formation. The pilot stated that after the left engine power loss, he engaged the carburetor heat; indicating that the pilot had not been utilizing the carburetor heat prior to the loss of engine power.
While it is possible that the loss of engine power to both engines was the result of carburetor icing, given the postaccident examination findings it is most likely that the left engine lost power after its fuel supply was exhausted. While the fuel tank feeding the right engine’s fuel supply had not yet been completely exhausted, it is likely that while maneuvering after the left engine loss of power, the right engine’s fuel tank pickup partially unported due to its low fuel level, resulting in its inconsistent delivery of fuel to that engine, a partial loss of power, and the airplane’s inability to maintain altitude.
20250604200265.fa:
HISTORY OF FLIGHTOn June 4, 2025, at 1341 eastern daylight time, a Piper PA-23, N2109P, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Palm Bay, Florida. The commercial pilot was uninjured and the passenger received minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
According to the owner/operator, the flight departed from Front Royal-Warren County Airport (FRR), Front Royal, Virginia, in the morning and was enroute to Boca Raton, Florida. According to the pilot, prior to departing FRR, he had filled both main fuel tanks with a total of 72 gallons of fuel. The pilot also reported that due to a fuel leak, the auxiliary fuel tanks were not used. The pilot reported making a fuel stop at the Orangeburg Municipal Airport (OGB), Orangeburg, South Carolina, where 60.3 gallons of fuel was added to top off the main fuel tanks. After departing OGB, the flight continued south. 
When the flight approached Savannah, Georgia, the pilot reported encountering a patch of weather and diverted to the west to go around it. After passing the weather, the pilot began to follow the coastline, and as the airplane approached the Daytona Beach area, the pilot diverted to the east to avoid another patch of weather. Shortly afterward, the pilot began an approach to their next fuel stop at Valkaria Airport (X59), Valkaria, Florida. While on approach to X59, the pilot reported entering a “massive rain shower,” and the pilot lost sight of the runway. The pilot aborted the approach and initiated a climb toward the east to exit the weather. 
After reaching about 1,500 ft mean sea level (msl), the pilot reported that the left engine began to sputter and lost power. The pilot applied carburetor heat and attempted to restart the left engine; however, engine power did not return. The pilot then reported that the right engine began to sputter. Unable to reach an airport, he elected to perform a forced ditching into the Indian River near Palm Bay, Florida. During the ditching, the airplane sustained substantial damage to the fuselage and empennage. The pilot and passenger exited the airplane and swam to shore. When asked how this accident could have been prevented, the pilot wrote that the “accident could have been prevented by landing sooner and filling up sooner” and noted that there were no mechanical malfunctions or failures that would have precluded normal operation. According to the PA-23 Operator’s Handbook, each main fuel tank had a capacity of 36 gallons, and each auxiliary fuel tank had a capacity of 18 gallons. A review of the Operator’s Handbook and the airplane’s Type Certificate Data Sheet (TCDS), revealed no indication of what the airplane’s unusable amount of fuel was. However, the TCDS indicated a similar airframe, the PA-23-250, had 1.7 gallons of fuel that were unusable. According to the pilot, he did not use the auxiliary fuel tanks due to fuel leaks. According to the FAA Special Airworthiness Information Bulletin CE-09-35, pilots “should be aware that carburetor icing doesn’t just occur in freezing conditions, it can occur at temperatures well above freezing temperatures when there is visible moisture or high humidity. Icing can occur in the carburetor at temperatures above freezing because vaporization of fuel, combined with the expansion of air as it flows through the carburetor, (Venturi Effect) causes sudden cooling, sometimes by a significant amount within a fraction of a second.” The bulletin also stated that pilots should be able to recognize the signs of carburetor icing, such as a drop in manifold pressure with constant speed airplanes and roughness in engine operation. The left fuel strainer bowl was removed and visually inspected; the strainer bowl cap was found to be severely corroded and displayed corrosion consistent with exfoliation corrosion. There was no fuel screen installed in the left fuel strainer, and the bowl contained several large pieces of corroded debris. 
The right main fuel tank cap was found to be secured to the fuel tank filler and was able to seal properly. The right auxiliary fuel tank cap was found installed in the right auxiliary tank filler; however, the right auxiliary tank filler neck was missing the metal ring insert that would allow the cap to seal properly. The right main fuel tank was drained at the fuel strainer, where approximately 1 gallon of water and 4 gallons of fuel with the odor and color consistent with 100LL Avgas were drained from the fuel tank. The right auxiliary fuel tank was found to be completely devoid of fluid.

The overhead components (valves, springs, and rocker arms) displayed normal operating and lubrication signatures and operated normally during crankshaft rotation. The carburetor was disassembled and the internal components were visually examined. The carburetor bowl was full of fluid consistent with water. On June 6, 2025, about 1830 central daylight time, an Air Tractor AT-502 airplane, N9185F, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Grady, Arkansas. The pilot was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 137 agricultural application flight.
The pilot was departing from a 2,300 ft long paved airstrip, oriented about 015°, at the time of the accident. A track in the grass off the right side of the runway began about 300 ft from the end of the pavement and appeared consistent with being made by the airplane tailwheel. The track was oriented about 025°.
After about 200 ft, the single track transitioned to three tracks consistent was all three landing gear wheels being on the ground. The tracks were about 200 ft long and ended about 100 ft beyond the end of the runway pavement. They continued along the approximate 025° heading into the adjacent soybean field. The center track was offset to the right relative to the outer two tracks consistent with the tail of the airplane being offset as it traveled through the bean field. An additional set of tracks began again about 50 ft from an irrigation ditch. The irrigation ditch was located about 450 ft from the end of the runway pavement.

Figure 1 – Runway with landing gear tracks

Figure 2 – Airplane at accident site along irrigation ditch
The airplane came to rest inverted on the north side of an irrigation. The outboard left wing was fragmented, and the aft fuselage was partially separated. The engine mount was deformed; however, the engine remained securely attached and appeared undamaged. Engine control continuity was confirmed.
Aileron control continuity was confirmed from the cockpit control stick to the left-wing pushrod and to the right aileron. The left aileron was separated and fragmented consistent with the outboard wing damage. Elevator control continuity was confirmed from the cockpit control stick to the elevators. However, the aft elevator pushrod was bent consistent with the fuselage damage. The left rudder cable was separated immediately forward of the rudder control horn. The separation was frayed consistent with an overstress failure. The right rudder cable was continuous from the cockpit rudder pedal to the control horn at the aft fuselage.
Further examination of the engine and airframe fuel system are planned. In addition, a Satloc GPS position tracking unit was retained for examination and download.

United Airlines flight 716, came to a sudden stop while taxiing out of the gate area and trying to make a turn onto taxiway C at Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport (PHX), Phoenix, Arizona. As a result of the abrupt stop, one flight attendant (FA) sustained a serious injury. The event flight returned to the gate and emergency medical services were called.

Flight 716 was a scheduled passenger flight from PHX to Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR), Newark, New Jersey, with a planned departure time of 0700 MST. The flight crew reported that this was the first flight of the day. The captain was the pilot flying, and the first officer (FO) was the pilot monitoring. According to the flight crew, there were no operational pressures, and following a normal pushback and engine start-up, the airplane was positioned on Taxiway Z facing north, holding short of Taxiway C, where they contacted Airport Traffic Control Tower (ATCT) ground control for taxi clearance (see figure 1).

Ground control issued the standard southbound taxi route, which they had reviewed during the pilot briefing. The captain confirmed the instructions with the FO that they would turn right on Taxiway C, then right on Taxiway S, holding short of Taxiway D. 

According to the flight crew, while taxiing at a speed below 10 knots, the FO noticed they were beginning to pass Taxiway C. The FO alerted the captain that they needed to turn right to enter Taxiway C. The captain applied the brakes to assist with the turning maneuver, using what he recalled felt like normal pressure. Initially, everything seemed normal, but shortly afterward, the flight crew indicated that they felt that the brakes responded more aggressively than expected, causing the airplane to come to an abrupt stop. Both crew members confirmed there was sufficient space to complete the turn safely.

Figure 1. Image of the taxi route for flight 716. (Source: United Airlines)

According to the forward FA’s, after the airplane had departed from the gate and was taxiing out to the runway, they had started showing the safety demonstration video. Shortly after that, the airplane came to an abrupt stop. Both FAs were in the forward galley at the time and were thrown into the metal counter and safety latches. Each reported experiencing sharp pain in the neck, back, and legs as a result of the sudden jolt. 

As the airplane entered Taxiway C, the flight crew received a call from one of the forward FA’s indicating that the other forward FA was injured and she needed to go back to the gate. The flight crew coordinated with PHX operations, ramp, and ground control to return to the gate. 

Paramedics met the airplane at the gate and transported the injured FA to the hospital where they were diagnosed with a serious injury.

According to United Airlines, their maintenance personnel conducted a post-accident general visual inspection of the airplane’s brake system and reported no anomalies were found. The airplane was subsequently placed on jacks, and the wheels were manually rotated. No evidence of brake dragging or grabbing was observed during this procedure. The brake system was cycled multiple times while the wheels were spun, and no faults or irregularities were identified. A review of maintenance history for this airplane showed that there were two maintenance entries for the braking system in the previous 90 days. Both entries were due to broken clips and were not related to braking actions.

On June 14, 2025, at 1245 eastern daylight time, a Beech 58 airplane, N82UC, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Tabor City, North Carolina. The private pilot and passenger were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
The instrument-rated private pilot departed on an instrument flight rules flight from Spartanburg Downtown Memorial Airport/Simpson Field (SPA), Spartanburg, South Carolina at 1120 and was enroute to Grand Strand Airport (CRE), North Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, which was located about 170 nautical miles (nm) to the southeast. 
Preliminary Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B) data and air traffic control communications showed that the enroute portion of the flight was normal and unremarkable. The pilot flew a track of about 100°, at an altitude of 7,000 ft mean sea level (msl), and 190 knots groundspeed; during this time the pilot was in communications with the Myrtle Beach (MYR) TRACON controller who issued the airport altimeter setting and queried the pilot if he had the current weather information. 
The controller instructed the pilot to descend and maintain 4,000 ft msl, which was acknowledged and complied with. The pilot requested a different heading because it looked like they would be heading “straight into” the weather and the controller subsequently issued a heading of 060°. Shortly after, the controller handed the pilot over to the eastern sector radar controller, who approved deviations left and right of course as needed. 
The pilot arrived in the vicinity of the airport and was preparing for an instrument approach. The controller approved additional deviations to the pilot as needed to avoid heavy precipitation and gave the pilot subsequent headings that would put the airplane on a heading to intercept the final approach course for the ILS approach to runway 23.
During this time, light rain was developing over CRE, and heavy precipitation had begun near the departure end of runway 23, along with wind gusts to 25 knots. The controller instructed the pilot to turn right to 140° and descend and maintain 1,700 ft msl. The pilot asked the controller to repeat the instructions which the controller did; the pilot acknowledged. Shortly after, the pilot was cleared for the ILS runway 23 approach and was instructed that in the event of a go-around, to fly heading 090° and maintain 2,000 ft msl, which was acknowledged.
As the airplane approached a 1 1/2-mile final, while descending through 800 ft msl, the pilot abandoned the approach and performed a left climbing turn to the north-northeast while climbing to 2,600 ft msl. The controller asked the pilot his intentions and the pilot responded by asking the controller to suggest a heading to get out of the weather and that they wanted to divert to Florence Regional Airport (FLO), Florence, South Carolina, about 55 nm to the west-northwest. The controller provided a heading of 350° and to maintain 3,000 ft msl. 
About 5 nm miles into the diversion, while at 3,000 ft msl, the pilot turned to a track of about 310° and began a descent; the airplane’s speed increased steadily from 160 knots to about 235 knots groundspeed in a steady straight-line descent. The controller attempted to contact the pilot; however, there was no response. Multiple transmissions were heard that included engine noise and inaudible conversation, but there was no direct pilot-to-controller communication from this point forward. No other communications were received, and radar contact was subsequently lost. The airplane’s descent rate went from -600 feet per minute (fpm) to -4,500 fpm until there was a brief arrest of the descent where it decreased to -300 fpm after which the descent rate increased again to -4,000 fpm until the ADS-B data ended. (Figure 1) During the final descent, there were no observed maneuvers or significant heading changes. The tree impact signatures at the accident site indicated a descent angle of about 23° and were consistent with the airplane being wings level. 
Figure 1 Final flight path through arrival, approach, diversion and accident.
The reported weather conditions at CRE about 5 minutes before the accident included wind from 240° at 20 knots gusting to 30 knots, 1 1/2-mile visibility with heavy thunderstorms, rain, and mist. There were few clouds at 1,000 ft above ground level (agl) and scattered clouds at 2,100 ft agl. The reported temperature and dewpoint were 27° and 26° C, respectively. 
At 1244, about the time of the accident, the reported wind was from 240° at 14 knots gusting to 27 knots, 3/4 mile visibility, heavy thunderstorms, rain and mist, few clouds at 800 ft, broken clouds at 1,800 ft and 5,000 ft agl and the reported temperature and dewpoint were 27° and 26° C, respectively.

Figure 2 Overview of final route of flight with flight track and weather.

The airplane impacted a remote and densely wooded area covered with 75 ft-tall mature pine trees at an elevation of 40 ft. The wreckage path was 468 ft-long and oriented on a magnetic heading of 293° and scattered in a tight formation throughout the entire path. The initial impact area was the tops of 75-ft-tall trees with associated tree and limb fractures progressively lower to the terrain; about 30 trees were damaged by the impact. The airplane wreckage was extremely fragmented. All flight control surfaces, wings, empennage, cockpit, and engine assemblies were impact-separated and strewn throughout the accident site. The largest item discovered at the accident site was a portion of the aft right fuselage that contained an entry step and door. There was no fire.
The accident site had the slight odor of aviation fuel and fuel blight was observed on the surrounding vegetation.
A majority of flight control surfaces and major components were identified and accounted for at the accident site, although all were severely fragmented and damaged. Flight control continuity could not be confirmed on site due to the severity of the damage; however, all control cables that were observed exhibited features consistent with tensile overload and a “broom straw” appearance. No indications of flight control anomalies were discovered during the accident site examination. Flight control trim settings were inconclusive. 
Both propeller assemblies separated from the engines and exhibited features consistent with impact and rotational damage. Both propellers showed signs of s-bends, chordwise scraping, leading edge gouges and trailing surface waves.
Both engines separated from their respective firewall and were impact-damaged and discovered in close proximity to each other. Both engines showed significant impact damage.
Two data cards were discovered in different locations at the accident site. The Garmin G1000 unit, which was severely damaged, was missing its data cards from their respective slots. The recovered cards were retained for examination and download. 
The wreckage was retained for further investigation.

Southwest Airlines flight 3508 encountered unanticipated moderate turbulence while deviating around convective weather. The flight originated from Dallas Love Field Airport (DAL), Dallas, Texas, with a planned destination of Northwest Florida Beaches International Airport (ECP), Panama City, Florida, and diverted to Jacksonville International Airport (JAX), Jacksonville, Florida. 
Preflight weather planning indicated scattered convective buildups in the Florida panhandle region, typical for that time of year. The crew designated JAX as the diversion airport. The flight departed DAL uneventfully, and en route operations were normal with the seat belt sign off and cabin service underway.
As the flight descended toward ECP, the flight crew received updated weather information showing developing convective activity near the airport. Air traffic control (ATC) vectors corresponded with what the crew saw via enroute weather monitoring. Another Southwest Airlines flight ahead of them executed a missed approach at ECP due to heavy precipitation and reduced visibility. 
The flight crew determined that available fuel on board would not permit multiple missed approaches and a diversion, so they elected to divert to JAX. According to the flight attendants (FAs), the seat belt sign was illuminated, and the flight crew reminded passengers to remain seated. However, a passenger disregarded the seat belt sign and entered the aft lavatory. During the climb to the east, through approximately 5,000 ft mean sea level in instrument meteorological conditions, the airplane encountered a brief period of moderate turbulence lasting 2 to 3 seconds. 
The autopilot disengaged, and the first officer assumed manual control. The flight crew stabilized the airplane and continued the diversion to JAX. When the airplane encountered turbulence, the passenger was exiting the aft lavatory and was thrown upward, striking the ceiling and the floor. The aft FA reported the passenger lost consciousness briefly before regaining awareness and sitting in the nearest available seat. The aft FA notified the flight crew of the injured passenger, and emergency medical personnel were requested to meet the airplane on arrival.
The flight landed uneventfully at JAX. Paramedics met the airplane and transported the injured passenger to a local hospital, where the passenger was diagnosed with multiple fractures to the neck and back and subsequently underwent surgery. No other injuries were reported and there was no damage to the airplane.

20250617200338.an:
The flight instructor and pilot-receiving-instruction were conducting a cross-country flight in the twin-engine turboprop airplane. According to the flight instructor, while in the airport traffic pattern at the destination airport, the pilot-receiving-instruction allowed the airplane to decelerate below a normal airspeed for the turn from base leg to final approach. He told the pilot-receiving-instruction to increase engine power to accelerate, but the airplane began to yaw left after the engine throttles were increased. The flight instructor “suspected that the left engine flamed out due to fuel starvation” and took control of the airplane. He retracted the landing gear and flaps, applied full right rudder, and rolled the airplane to the right into the operating right engine. The flight instructor did not feather the left propeller because he believed the left engine was still producing limited thrust. The airplane continued in the left turn despite the flight instructor’s corrective actions. The fight instructor did not attempt to turn the airplane back toward the runway because he believed the airplane was accelerating and would clear the hangar ahead of them. The airplane impacted the hangar and came to rest on the roof.

The airplane sustained substantial damage to the lower fuselage, both wings, and the right engine separated from the mounts. There was no evidence of a fuel spill in, on, or around the hangar. Examination of the airplane fuel tanks confirmed they were not breached during the accident. When drained, the left- and right-wing fuel tanks contained about 3 fluid ounces and about 30 fluid ounces of fuel, respectively.

Although the flight instructor and pilot-receiving-instruction provided different accounts of how much fuel was present before the flight, both pilots stated that the indicated fuel level was within the yellow caution band on both fuel tank gauges before departure. According to the Beech E90 airplane flight manual, takeoffs are prohibited when the fuel tank gauge indications are within the yellow caution band (0 to 260 lbs). Ultimately, the exact amount of fuel available before the flight could not be determined with any certainty. The flight instructor estimated that the 16-minute flight required between 135 to 200 lbs of fuel. The flight instructor opined that the fuel tank gauges were inaccurate which resulted in fuel exhaustion to the left engine.

Review of ADS-B flight track data revealed the airplane decelerated below minimum controllable airspeed (VMC) during the turn from base leg to final approach. The airplane continued to decelerate during the go-around. The flight instructor stated that the accident could have been prevented had the airplane’s best single-engine rate-of-climb airspeed (VYSE) been maintained until the runway and landing were ensured. Based on the amount of fuel recovered after the accident, there was likely insufficient fuel remaining to perform a go-around and reenter the traffic pattern for landing with one engine operating.

United Airlines flight 2857, from George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH), Houston, Texas to Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport (FLL), Fort Lauderdale, Florida, encountered unanticipated turbulence during descent. Two flight attendants (FAs) sustained serious injuries, one sustained a minor injury, and there were no passenger injuries. 
According to the flight crew, the captain, who was the pilot flying, reported that prior to departure from Houston, he conducted a turbulence mitigation briefing with the cabin crew emphasizing expected callouts and seating times. The flight was delayed approximately two hours due to thunderstorms and ramp closures at IAH. Departure and cruise were uneventful.
During descent through approximately 35,000 feet (FL350), the seat belt sign was turned on. The FO, acting as pilot monitoring, made the public address (PA) to passengers and instructed the cabin crew to “prepare the cabin for landing” while descending through about 31,000 feet. According to both pilots, no turbulence was reported by air traffic control, and onboard weather radar and turbulence detection systems indicated no significant activity. The flight was operating in and out of instrument meteorological conditions (IMC) at the time.
While descending through approximately FL250, the captain observed green and yellow radar returns rapidly developing directly ahead of the airplane. Before the flight crew could request for deviations, the airplane encountered a sudden, brief episode of moderate turbulence lasting approximately 3 to 5 seconds. The autopilot remained engaged, and the airplane remained in positive control throughout. The FO immediately made a PA announcement instructing the cabin crew to be seated.
Following the turbulence encounter, the purser contacted the flight deck to report that three FAs had been injured. FA2, located in the aft galley, was thrown upward and landed on her left foot, sustaining a serious foot injury. FA3, while securing the aft lavatory, fell to the lavatory floor during the turbulence, twisting her left ankle and sustaining a serious injury. FA4, positioned in the forward galley, was thrown into the 1L door, later diagnosed with sprains and contusions. 
Two medical professionals on board assisted and examined the injured FAs during the remainder of the flight. The flight crew coordinated with dispatch and Fort Lauderdale operations to have emergency medical personnel meet the airplane upon arrival and provide medical attention to the injured FAs. The three injured FAs were transported to a local hospital. There were no other injuries, and the airplane was not damaged.

The pilot departed in the float-equipped airplane to perform three water and three land landings for currency purposes. During the approach to the glassy surface of the rural freshwater lake, the floats impacted the lake. The pilot reported that a “hard impact” occurred, and the float attachment struts were damaged. During the impact, the pilot believed the airplane was between 20 to 25 ft above the glassy surface of the lake. The airplane came to rest upright, and the pilot was able to egress from the cockpit onto a float. The pilot was then picked up by an individual in a nearby boat. Shortly after, the airplane partially sank, and it came to rest inverted in the lake.
The airplane sustained substantial damage to the fuselage. The pilot reported there were no preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airframe or the engine that would have precluded normal operation. The pilot further reported that the accident could have been prevented by remembering that it is “almost impossible to judge height above glassy water.” The FAA Aeronautical Information Manual (AIM) discusses various illusions leading to landing errors. The FAA AIM defines the featureless terrain illusion as, “an absence of ground features, as when landing over water, darkened areas, and terrain made featureless by snow, can create the illusion that the aircraft is at a higher altitude than it actually is.”

The pilot and the passenger were attempting to take off when surveillance video captured, and a witness heard, the sound of the airplane’s engine backfiring followed by a sudden decrease and increase in engine power. Dark smoke was also seen trailing under the belly of the airplane. Data downloaded from the airplane’s onboard engine monitor recorded an rpm drop from 2,600 to 1,500 rpm then back to 2,500 rpm shortly after the airplane became airborne. Fuel flow, manifold pressure, and horsepower readings uniformly tracked with the decrease/increase of rpm, consistent with the pilot quickly reducing the throttle to idle then back to full power. During the takeoff, the pilot advised the air traffic controller that the airplane was having an engine problem and that he planned to “head up and turn back.” The airplane subsequently made a right turn toward the intersecting runway shortly after the engine backfired and it’s possible the pilot reduced power in an attempt to land but changed his mind and decided to circle back to another runway. The airplane then entered a steep left turn and descended, in what a witness described as a stall-like state. The last radar return indicated the airplane was about 110 ft above the ground at a groundspeed near its published stall speed. According to data downloaded from the airplane’s engine monitor, the engine was operating near full power as the airplane descended to ground contact.
Postaccident examination of the engine revealed the No. 2 cylinder bottom spark plug was loose, and stains/residue from combustion exhaust gas leakage was visible around the spark plug port consistent that it had been loose prior to the accident. Review of the airplane’s engine maintenance logbook revealed that the spark plugs were, “cleaned, gapped, tested, and rotated” at the last annual inspection, about 37 hours before the accident. There were no other entries in the engine maintenance logbook regarding removal of the spark plugs after the annual inspection. According to the engine manufacturer’s service instruction on how to install spark plugs, the spark plugs should have been torqued to a specific torque value to prevent them from coming loose. 
Examination of the fuel system and its components revealed evidence of water/corrosion and debris; however, testing found no indication that would have precluded fuel from reaching the engine. While the data showed that the cylinder head temperature was low on the No. 1 cylinder, there was no evidence of a stuck valve, and the ignition system tested normally. An erratic exhaust gas temperature (EGT) reading for the No. 1 cylinder was also recorded for the entire flight. The EGT data had been erratic since the engine’s last annual inspection. The No.1 cylinder’s EGT connector was found undamaged and the yellow (positive) wire for the EGT probe was not connected (the red wire was connected). As such, the probe had most likely not been working properly since the last annual inspection. 
Based on the available information, it is most likely that the backfiring heard coming from the engine was due to the loose No. 2 cylinder spark plug, which was not properly torqued at the last annual inspection. Despite the fact that the engine was still producing close to full power following the backfire, the pilot entered a steep turn, likely in an attempt to return to the airport, after which the airplane most likely stalled from an altitude that was too low to recover.

HISTORY OF FLIGHTOn June 19, 2025, at 0847 eastern daylight time, a Mooney M20F, N9573M, was involved in an accident near Beverly, Massachusetts. The commercial pilot/owner and the passenger were fatally injured. The flight was conducted as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
A review of air traffic control tower communications and radar data provided by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) revealed the airplane was cleared for takeoff at 0845 from runway 16 at Beverly Municipal Airport (BVY), Beverly, Massachusetts. According to the tower controller on duty, when the airplane was about 500 ft above the runway, he observed dark smoke trailing under the belly of the airplane. The controller asked the pilot if everything was okay and cleared him to land on any runway. The pilot responded he was having engine trouble, and they were going to “head up and turn back.” The controller cleared the pilot to land on runway 09. The control said the airplane initially turned right toward runway 09, then turned left. The airplane continued banking to the left into a steeper turn and descended behind trees.
A witness, who was a flight instructor at BVY, watched the airplane depart. He said there was a “significant reduction in power” when the airplane reached 150 ft agl and was about halfway down the 5,001-ft-long runway. He said, “A few seconds later it seemed as though the engine got power back partially. The pilot initiated a left turn to the east.” While turning the engine sounded as though there was another significant reduction in power. The airplane then began to descend with its wings level eventually in what appeared to be a “stalled” state behind the tree line to the accident site.
Airport security video captured the airplane shortly after it became airborne, and dark smoke could be seen trailing under the airplane. The video, which had no sound, showed the airplane initially turning to the right before it turned left. The airplane then entered a steep turn and descended behind trees.
Another surveilence camera located at the airport captured the sound of the airplane as it was departing and the last few moments of the flight before impact. About 0846:28, the sound of the airplane taking off was heard followed by the sound of the engine backfiring at 1846:32. The sound of engine power then quickly decreased before a suddenly increase. The airplane appeared to continue to climb with the engine running before it entered a very steep left turn to the northeast. The airplane descended and disappeared behind trees. 
The last radar return received on the airplane was at 0846:55. At that time, the airplane was 217 ft mean sea level (110 ft above ground level) at a ground speed of 65 knots (see figure 1).

Figure 1 - The airplane’s final two radar-derived positions with the wreckage location/accident site annotated. PERSONNEL INFORMATIONThe pilot held a commercial pilot certificate with ratings for airplane single-engine land and instrument airplane. His most-recent FAA second-class medical certificate was issued on September 2, 2020, without limitations. A review of the pilot’s logbook revealed that his last logged flight was on April 4, 2025. At that time, he had logged 429 total flight hours of which, 77.2 hours were in the accident airplane. AIRCRAFT INFORMATIONThe airplane’s last annual inspection of the engine was completed on October 11, 2024, about 37 hours prior to the accident. At the time of the accident, the engine had accrued a total of 2,268.9 hours and 553.7 hours since overhaul. 
A laminated Emergency Checklist was found in the wreckage. According to the checklist, the first item listed after losing engine power immediately after takeoff was to maintain an airspeed of 100 miles per hour (mph) or 87 knots indicated airspeed.
According to the airplane’s owner’s manual, the stall speed of the airplane with 15 degree of flaps extended (takeoff flap setting) in wings level flight (0-degree bank) and landing gear retracted was 64 mph or approximately 55 knots. The stall speed rose to roughly 93 mph (approx. 80 knots) in a 60° bank. AIRPORT INFORMATIONThe airplane’s last annual inspection of the engine was completed on October 11, 2024, about 37 hours prior to the accident. At the time of the accident, the engine had accrued a total of 2,268.9 hours and 553.7 hours since overhaul. 
A laminated Emergency Checklist was found in the wreckage. According to the checklist, the first item listed after losing engine power immediately after takeoff was to maintain an airspeed of 100 miles per hour (mph) or 87 knots indicated airspeed.
According to the airplane’s owner’s manual, the stall speed of the airplane with 15 degree of flaps extended (takeoff flap setting) in wings level flight (0-degree bank) and landing gear retracted was 64 mph or approximately 55 knots. The stall speed rose to roughly 93 mph (approx. 80 knots) in a 60° bank. WRECKAGE AND IMPACT INFORMATIONThe airplane impacted a grass berm adjacent to a two-lane road with the left wing, then crossed the road and impacted a light pole where it came to rest upright and perpendicular to the road. There was no postimpact fire. The left wing separated from the airframe and was found about 15 to 20 ft forward and to the right of the main wreckage. The wing tip, aileron, and flap had separated, and the fuel tank was breached; however, when the fuel tank cap was removed, fuel was observed about 3-inches below the tab. The tail section separated from the airframe and came to rest to the left of the fuselage. The engine and propeller assembly remained partially attached to the firewall and was displaced about 70 degrees to the left. The right wing (including the aileron and flap) remained secure to its respective wing root. The right flap appeared to be extended about 15 degrees (takeoff setting), and the landing gear were retracted. The right wing fuel tank was not breached and about 32 gallons of 100LL were visually observed when the fuel tank cap was removed.
The airplane’s flight control tubes were fractured in several locations due to impact; however, continuity was established for all major flight controls to the cockpit area. 
The airplane was equipped with two Electronics International engine monitors; however, only one monitor recorded the accident flight. Data downloaded from the monitor revealed that during the last 25 seconds of the flight, the engine rpm dropped from 2,600 to 1,500 before it increased back to 2,600 and settled at 2,500 rpm. Fuel flow, manifold pressure and engine-horsepower readings all uniformly followed the decrease and increase of rpm. Just before the data ended, there was another small reduction/increase in fuel flow and rpm that coincided with an increase in the No. 2 thru 4-cylinder exhaust gas (EGT) temperatures.
The data also indicated that the No. 1 cylinder EGT reading was erratic for the entire accident flight and had been erratic since the date of the last annual inspection in October 2024. Examination of photos taken of the No. 1 cylinder at the accident site revealed the OLC-2 connector for the K-type EGT probe was not damaged. However, the yellow (positive) wire was disconnected from the connector, and the red (negative) wire was connected. The yellow wire not being connected would result in erratic EGT readings.
The engine was separated from the airframe for examination. The top spark plugs were removed from the engine, and the plugs appeared dark in color. The engine’s crankshaft rotated freely via manual rotation of the propeller, and compression/valve train continuity were established on each cylinder. The compression was low on the No. 2 cylinder compared to the other cylinders. The engine sustained impact damage and the No. 2 cylinder intake tube had been pushed into the No. 2 cylinder bottom spark plug. The spark plug exhibited a slight bend. 
Further examination revealed that the No. 2 bottom spark plug was loose and the area around the plug port exhibited dark combustion exhaust leakage as evidence by staining/residue on the exterior and cooling fins, consistent with the plug being loose at the time of impact (figure 2). The spark plug’s position was marked and when it was manually moved to a hand tight position (or zero-torque position), it took about 1/8th to 1/4 - inch turn to do so. When it was attempted to tighten the spark plug to facilitate better compression, the plug broke at the base of the threaded section that housed the electrodes as soon as torque was applied. The broken spark plug was examined by the NTSB Materials Laboratory, and the fracture surfaces were consistent with overstress. No preexisting anomalies were identified. The No. 2 cylinder top sparkplug was installed in the bottom port, and a another compression test was performed. The compression was consistent with the other cylinders.

Figure 2 - Combustion exhaust leakage stains and residue around the No. 2 cylinder bottom spark plug port.
Review of the airplane’s engine maintenance logbook revealed that the spark plugs were, “cleaned, gapped, tested, and rotated” at the last annual inspection in October 2024. There were no other entries in the engine maintenance logbook regarding the removal of the sparkplugs after the annual inspection.
According to Lycoming Service Instruction 1042AH, which was active at the time of the accident, Spark Plug Installation Guidelines, the installation torque values were:
All spark plugs - 420 in.-lbs. (or 35 ft.-lbs.) (47.5 Nm)
5/8-24 (16 mm-24) lead nuts - 80 to 90 in.-lbs. (9 to 10 Nm)
3/4-20 (19 mm-20) lead nuts - 110 to 120 in.-lbs. (12 to 13.6 Nm)
The magnetos remained secured in the accessory housing. A timing check was performed; the left magneto timing was late, near top dead center. The left magneto flange was fractured and appeared to have shifted during the impact sequence. The magneto was removed, the drive was secure, and it sparked from all four posts when the impulse coupling was snapped by hand. 
The right magneto was secure to the engine and was correctly timed. The magneto was removed, the drive was secure, and spark was observed from all four posts when the drive was rotated with a drill.
The fuel selector was found on the right-wing fuel tank. When the selector was moved by hand, it moved freely to the “left” and “off” detents. The firewall fuel strainer was removed, and a small amount of debris and water were in the bowl. A few strings of unidentified debris were on the screen.
Per the M20F Owner’s Manual, the electric boost pump was to be turned on for takeoff; however, the toggle switch on the instrument panel was found in the off position. During the postaccident examination, when power was applied to the pump, and the pump motor operated. 
The fuel line from the boost pump to the main fuel supply line to the engine was breached from impact. When compressed air was blown through the main fuel line at each wing root, fuel sprayed out of the lines at the fuel selector strainer indicating that fuel was capable of reaching the fuel selector from both tanks. The breached fuel lines and the main fuel supply line to the engine were also clear of debris. 
The fuel injector servo was removed from the engine, and clear 100LL fuel was drained from the servo body. The fuel screen was removed and absent of debris. The fuel manifold was removed along with the fuel injectors. When the No. 3 fuel injector was removed, the insert separated. The injector and insert were clear of debris. All of the other injectors/inserts were clear of debris. The manifold was disassembled, and fuel was in the manifold body. The fuel was absent of debris/water and the diaphragm was intact. 
The fuel servo and manifold were removed and sent out to the manufacturer to be bench tested. A small amount of water, corrosion and sand-like debris were found in the servo; however, the servo and manifold/injectors tested to manufacturer specifications. 
The fuel pump remained secured to the engines accessory housing. The fuel pump was removed, and fuel was present in the fuel pump. It created pressure, and suction when the lever was actuated. The pump was disassembled and a white sealant-like material was observed in the fuel outlet chamber and pump chamber. Evidence of corrosion was also observed in both chambers. 
The oil filter adapter broke from engine due to impact, and the back of engine was covered with oil. The filter was absent any metallic debris. The oil sump screen was removed and absent of any debris. 
The air filter was clean.
The engine monitor also indicated that the cylinder head temperature (CHT) for the No. 1 cylinder had a consistent low temperature reading for the entire flight of about 275 degrees F. A lighted borescope was used to examine the interior of the No. 1 cylinder, and no evidence of a stuck valve was observed. The cylinder’s valve guide was measured using a Lycoming valve gage guide (R-ST-310). The test indicated the valve’s play was tight and below minimums per Lycoming Service Bulletin 388. The No. 1 cylinder was then removed from the engine along with the remaining cylinders for comparison.
The interior walls of the No. 1, 2, and 3 cylinders exhibited some lead bromide deposits. The interior walls of the No. 4 cylinder appeared new (replaced at the last annual) and did not exhibit any lead bromide deposits.
The exhaust valve was removed from the No. 1 cylinder. The valve was easily removed from the cylinder, and no deposits were observed on the valve stem. No mechanical deficiencies or malfunctions were observed that would have contributed to the low CHT reading. MEDICAL AND PATHOLOGICAL INFORMATIONAn autopsy was conducted on the pilot by the Commonwealth of Massachusetts, Office of the Chief Medical Examiner on July 20, 2025. The cause of death was determined to be multiple blunt force injuries as the manner of death to be an accident.
Toxicology testing performed at the FAA Forensic Sciences Laboratory identified Minoxidil in the pilot’s urine. Minoxidil is a medication commonly used to stimulate hair growth.

American Airlines flight 1286 (AAL1286) encountered unexpected convectively induced turbulence (CIT) while at 25,000 ft (FL250) about 17 minutes after departure from Miami International Airport (MIA), Miami, Florida. One flight attendant (FA) received a serious injury, and 3 FAs and 6 passengers received minor injuries. The seatbelt sign was illuminated at the time of the event. No significant convective weather or turbulence was forecasted or depicted during the flight crew’s flight planning or displayed on the onboard weather radar, or WSI weather app before the event. 
At the time of the event, multiple FAs were conducting cabin service with beverage carts positioned in the aisle, and one passenger was occupying the aft lavatory. The turbulence lasted about 5 to 8 seconds and consisted of abrupt vertical accelerations, resulting in multiple FAs being thrown to the floor or striking interior cabin structures, unsecured service items becoming airborne, and damage to the aft lavatory door.
AAL1286 flight crew indicated they had the airborne radar tilt up to 3.5 degrees during the period and likely scanned over the area. Airborne radar does not detect echoes less than 20 dBZ, while echoes of 45 dBZ were detected under the flight track. The model High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) sounding indicated a potential for updrafts to 144 knots or 4,173 fpm, and an unstable atmosphere. 
Following the turbulence encounter, the captain transferred control to the first officer and communicated with the cabin crew to assess injuries. A deadheading captain assisted with cabin coordination and injury assessment. The flight crew contacted dispatch and MedLink and declared an emergency with air traffic control. Based on medical guidance and aircraft position, the decision was made to continue to Raleigh-Durham International Airport (RDU), North Carolina. The airplane landed without further incident. Emergency medical personnel met the flight upon arrival at RDU, and injured crew members and at least one passenger were transported to local hospitals for evaluation and treatment. One FA was diagnosed with a fracture to her arm.
A review of the weather conditions indicated that there were no frontal boundaries over the area and no organized jet streams or strong winds aloft to indicate any potential clear air turbulence (CAT). While the NWS convective outlook expected a widely scattered area of general thunderstorms over Florida and the surrounding coastal waters during the time period. The High-level Significant Weather Prognostic Chart indicated no organized areas of convection or turbulence over the general route of flight, and no PIREPs or inflight weather advisories for thunderstorms or turbulence were current at the time of the turbulence encounter. 
A review of the NWS weather surveillance radar 1988 doppler (WSR88D) and satellite imagery showed an area of scattered echoes over central Florida and off the Florida coast between the Bahamas Islands. A review of the flight path confirmed that the flight over flew an area of developing echoes near 45 dBZ which rapidly increased in height between FL250 to FL420 surrounding the period, while the GOES-19 infrared image indicated radiative cloud tops near FL380 at the time of the turbulence encounter. Several cloud-to-ground lightning strikes were noted with the echoes after the flight had overflown the area of echoes. Thus, other than the flight’s airborne weather radar no visual clues were available prior to the encounter.
A HRRR numerical model indicated an unstable atmosphere with potential strong updrafts or maximum vertical velocities (MVV) near to 14,173 fpm. The Eddy Dissipation Rate (EDR) recorded by the accident flight was 0.665 which corresponded to the upper bounds of severe turbulence for a medium weight category aircraft. 
A review of the astronomical conditions indicated that official nighttime conditions existed at the time of the encounter with no illumination from the Moon, which was more than 30 degrees below the horizon at the time of the encounter.

The pilot planned to land near a restaurant for lunch with three passengers. He over flew the landing area and then set up for a “gradual and slow” approach. When the helicopter touched down, he felt the tail drop backwards. The pilot stated that he compensated by adding collective and forward cyclic which inadvertently induced a dynamic rollover. He added that a gusty tailwind prevailed at the time of the landing.

The helicopter sustained damage to the main rotor blades, the main rotor transmission mount, fuselage, and horizontal stabilizers. The pilot reported that there were no mechanical malfunctions or failures associated with the helicopter before the accident.

The pilot reported that, as he neared his destination, he became distracted by worsening weather conditions and forgot to switch fuel tanks. As a result, the fuel was depleted from the right fuel tank, and the airplane suffered a total loss of engine power. While attempting to restart the engine, the pilot intended to the move the selector to the left tank, but inadvertently moved the fuel selector from the right tank to the off position instead. Unable to restart the engine, the pilot selected a field to perform a forced landing. Prior to touchdown, the pilot realized the fuel was selected off and moved the fuel selector to the left tank; however, before power could be restored, the airplane impacted terrain, resulting in substantial damage to the wings, fuselage, and empennage.
The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.

The pilot was returning to his home-base airport after some minor maintenance to the airplane’s emergency locator transmitter. The preflight checks and run-up were normal and he performed a short-field takeoff from a 2,895-ft-long turf runway. As the airplane lifted off and began to climb, engine power decreased. The pilot ensured that the throttle and mixture controls were full forward, but the engine only retained partial power and he was unable to maintain altitude. The pilot subsequently landed the airplane hard on level terrain off the airport property, collapsing the landing gear and resulting in substantial damage to the airframe and right wing.
Postaccident examination of the engine revealed that the throttle cable sleeve had separated from a connection where it was crimped to secure it. Forward movement of the throttle would result in the cable forming a “U” shape and remaining slack. With the throttle in this position, the engine was likely unable to produce sufficient power to continue the climb. The examination identified no other evidence of a mechanical malfunction or failure that would have precluded normal operation.
Although the engine had been overhauled and reinstalled about a year before the accident, review of maintenance records showed no documentation that a new throttle cable assembly was installed, nor was it required to be. The preexisting engine throttle cable was reattached after the overhaul, inspected, and exercised with no anomalies observed. Additionally, no maintenance to the throttle controls had been documented in the logs between the time of the engine overhaul and the accident. Given the available information, it is likely that the single crimp holding the throttle sleeve in place became loose and detached, which resulted in the throttle moving to a low power position and did not allow the pilot to control the throttle after it separated.
20250623200380.fa:
On June 23, 2025, about 0935 eastern daylight time, a Cessna R182 airplane, N262AL, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Milton, Florida. The airline transport pilot and pilot-rated passenger were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 positioning flight.
The pilot departed from Dothan Regional Airport (DHN), Dothan, Alabama, and flew to J22 Ranch Airport (16FL), Milton, Florida, to have a new emergency locator transmitter battery installed. About 90 minutes after arriving, the maintenance was completed, and the pilot departed for the flight back to DHN. The pilot reported that he conducted preflight checks and a run-up, then performed a short-field takeoff from runway 36, a 2,895-ft turf runway. After the takeoff roll and rotation, the pilot began the initial climb and retracted the landing gear. The airplane was about 100 ft over the runway when the engine started losing power. The pilot stated that the engine retained partial power, but that it was not enough to maintain altitude.
The pilot attempted to troubleshoot the loss of engine power; he checked to make sure the throttle and mixture were full forward, but was unable to regain full power. The pilot subsequently landed off the departure end of the runway and slightly east of the centerline. During the final approach, he held the nose up and landed hard on the level terrain. The impact collapsed the right main landing gear and the airplane skidded to a stop, resulting in substantial damage to the airframe. 
Postaccident examination of the airplane revealed that the right wing tip was crushed upward, and there was buckling of the wings and fuselage. The 3-blade metal propeller was slightly curled on the outer 12 inches of the blades. The pilot reported that there were 65 gallons of 100LL aviation fuel on board at takeoff.
During a subsequent engine examination, the engine crankshaft was manually rotated by the propeller, which confirmed continuity of the powertrain. Thumb compression and suction were achieved on all cylinders. The magnetos sparked on all leads when the input drives were rotated. A lighted boroscope was used to examine all 6 cylinders; no anomalies were observed. During a functional check of the throttle, mixture, and propeller controls, it was revealed that the throttle control end had pulled out of the plunger guide. Manual operation of the throttle did not activate full throttle control to the engine. There was about a 2 1/2 -inch detachment of the throttle plunger and cable where the unit was separated. The line was slack when the throttle was moved to the full power setting, which would have resulted in the engine in a partial power condition (see figure). 

Figure - Throttle control end and plunger diagram from illustrated parts catalog and photograph of detached throttle cable and plunger. Note the single crimp at the yellow arrow and the area where it should be secured. Yellow circles identify parts affected. 
A review of maintenance records revealed that on October 3, 2022, the engine was removed for overhaul. This included the installation of an overhauled Marvel-Schebler carburetor 10-5235 (Model HA-6). The zero-timed engine was reinstalled, along with magnetos, a new starter and fuel pump. There was no replacement of the throttle cable assembly during reinstallation on March 21, 2024. A subsequent engine run and break-in revealed no defects, and the records indicated that no further maintenance related to the throttle was performed before the accident. A mechanic with inspection authorization who worked on the airframe after the overhauled engine was reinstalled stated that the throttle cable assembly was reconnected to the engine. The subsequent inspection included a visual inspection of the cable controls to ensure proper and secured rigging followed by an exercise of the system; it was manually actuated through the throttle to ensure there was no binding and smooth operation.

find: Aircraft-Aircraft propeller/rotor-Propeller system-Propeller hub section-Not serviced/maintained
20250623200381.an:
The pilot was returning to his home airport at an altitude of about 2,000 ft msl. He reported that there was a sudden and violent vibration throughout the airplane that lasted several seconds. The airplane’s canopy unlatched and opened due to the vibration and the engine lost power immediately afterward. The pilot established the airplane’s best glide speed and instructed the passenger to set the transponder to 7700 and to hold the canopy closed. The pilot conducted an emergency landing to a field. During the landing on uneven terrain, the right main landing gear collapsed, followed by the nose landing gear, and the right wing contacted the ground before the airplane came to rest. During a postaccident interview, the pilot reported that he realized the propeller had failed in flight. The airplane’s fuselage was substantially damaged during the accident sequence.
Postaccident examination of the airplane revealed that two of the three wood/composite propeller blades were separated from the propeller hub. The blades were not recovered and thus could not be examined. According to the propeller manufacturer, the propeller was required to be overhauled every 300 flight hours, or 5 (calendar) years, whichever came first. Review of the airplane’s maintenance records revealed that the new propeller had been installed onto the airplane nearly 7 years and nearly 510 hours before the accident. There were no entries documenting that the propeller had undergone the prescribed overhaul during that time. Given this information, it is likely that the propeller blades separated in flight, and that the failure of the propeller blades was due to an exceedance of the manufacturer’s overhaul requirement.
